# NU Institutional Investment Thesis — 31 August 2026

# PART I — INVESTMENT COMMITTEE DECISION

## 1. One-Line Decision

Decision: **Avoid** — Nu is growing quickly, but every engine-derived 12-month fair-value case is below the US$14.30 NYSE price, while the evidence needed to prove the discount rate and bank-specific survival case is incomplete.

## 3. Would I Buy This With Real Money Today?

Final answer: **I would not buy NU today**. Q2 operating momentum is real, but the price asks the investor to resolve the largest valuation uncertainty in Nu's favor. The valuation module's bull/base/bear values are US$8.43/US$6.47/US$4.40, all below US$14.30. The weighted scenario set adds a genuine US$18.78 positive tail and still produces a US$7.472 target and -47.7483% expected return. [analyses/NU_2026-08-31/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md, §§1–7, 2026-08-31]; [data/NU/NuHoldingsLtdNYSENUEstimatesReport.xls, Capital IQ Estimates, Target Price, export 2026-08-29].

- **Confidence:** 52.0/100 conviction; 69.5/100 understanding.
- **Position stance:** no position. An Avoid is not authorization to short.
- **What would raise confidence in the Avoid:** a group-wide, post-tax USD cost of equity materially above 9.78%, plus Q3 evidence that the raised bar and risk expansion are not durable.
- **What would lower confidence:** a defensible group cost of equity at or below 9.78%, or a material Q3 revenue/EPS beat with stable or better credit metrics on the same basis.
- **What would force rejection of the Avoid:** the kill criteria in §10, especially rate reconciliation or repeated earnings outperformance without credit deterioration.

## 4. The Actual Variant Perception

- **What everyone already knows:** Nu is a fast-growing Latin American digital bank. Q2 2026 had 139 million customers, 83.5% activity, US$17 monthly ARPAC (average revenue per active customer), 50.3% revenue growth, and 66.3% diluted-EPS growth. [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_Preliminary_Interim_Report(Aug-13-2026).pdf, Q2 2026, slides 6 and 15–16]; [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_Interim_Report(Aug-14-2026).pdf, Q2/H1 2026, p.5].
- **What is probably priced in:** the US$14.30 price and US$18.78 mean sell-side target give credit for continued high growth and returns. At a 16.51% cost of equity, the price requires 47.36% terminal ROE or 80.89% FY2027–30 profit growth; the price also reconciles at a 9.78% cost of equity. [analyses/NU_2026-08-31/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md, §§1–7, 2026-08-31]; [data/NU/NuHoldingsLtdNYSENUEstimatesReport.xls, Capital IQ Estimates, Target Price, export 2026-08-29].
- **What the engine thinks may be missed:** current spread and revenue gains depend heavily on credit income before the full credit-loss outcome is visible; H1 net income also included a US$991.046 million deferred-tax benefit. This makes the current earnings run-rate less cash-backed than the headline growth suggests. It does not prove improper accounting. [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_Interim_Report(Aug-14-2026).pdf, H1 2026, pp.5, 12 and 36–37]; [analyses/NU_2026-08-31/earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md, §§3–8, 2026-08-30].
- **What evidence proves we are actually different:** the edge would be proven only if a sourced group-wide cost of equity is materially above 9.78% and the Q3 2026 filing misses the raised revenue/EPS bar or shows worse credit quality. It is falsified if a defensible group rate is at or below 9.78% and Q3 produces a material dual beat with stable or better credit metrics.

**Edge score: 45/100. There is no proven variant perception yet.** The filing evidence supports a skeptical earnings-quality read, but the central valuation rate is not group-wide and sell-side target-price evidence points the other way.

## 5. Thesis → Antithesis → Final Thesis

- **Thesis:** Nu's reach, activity, revenue growth, and Q2 spread improvement show a digital lender gaining scale and extracting more value per customer.
- **Antithesis:** the valuation already assumes exceptional returns, the FQ3 bar is high, risk expansion precedes the final loss outcome, and part of H1 net income came from deferred tax.
- **Revised thesis:** the business can keep growing and the stock can still be a poor purchase at US$14.30; operating quality and valuation are separate questions.
- **Final thesis:** avoid owning NU at the current price. Do not short because the group discount rate is unresolved, consensus retains a US$18.78 positive tail, and no borrow/options evidence was supplied.
- **Insight threshold:** Insight threshold reached: the remaining uncertainty is mostly data-dependent, not reasoning-dependent.

## 6. Simple Summary

- Nu is a digital bank/lender serving consumers and small businesses in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia; interest and financial-instrument gains supplied 85.2% of FY2025 revenue. [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_20-F(Apr-08-2026).pdf, FY2025, Item 5, pp.157–158].
- The good news is scale and use: 139 million customers, 83.5% active, and US$17 monthly ARPAC in Q2 2026.
- The bad news is price: the valuation module's US$8.43 bull value is still 41.0% below US$14.30.
- Q2 revenue and EPS grew 50.3% and 66.3%, but Q3 consensus already requires 42.3% and 39.0% growth.
- The Q2 risk-adjusted-NIM gain was real, but 178bp of the 294bp rise came from credit income and 115bp from lower credit cost; a 1bp residual remains. Later losses can reverse some of that gain.
- The balance-sheet-survival module could not apply a corporate debt/EBITDA framework to this regulated lender. That is an intentional data gap, not proof of distress.
- Buy now or wait: **wait**. At US$14.30, no engine fair-value case offers a cushion.
- The highest-value decision input is a sourced NU Group cost of equity reconciled to the 16.51% Brazil-CGU rate and the 9.78% market-implied rate. The balance module separately needs primary-regulator prudential returns to complete a survival read.

## 6. Valuation and Peer Mispricing

The valuation module owns the levels. The 12-month fair values are **US$8.43 bull, US$6.47 base, and US$4.40 bear**. Forward price-to-tangible-book value (P/TBV — price paid for each dollar of tangible equity) sets the scenario cases; the US$6.47 base equally blends a US$7.38 peer next-twelve-month P/E value and US$5.55 residual-income value. The weighted primary methods are 33% apart; the full US$2.95–US$7.92 field spans 168%. These are not independent confirmations because the peer methods share a bank peer set. [analyses/NU_2026-08-31/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md, §§1–7, 2026-08-31].

| Metric | Company | Peer Median / Anchor | Premium / Discount | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Vendor-basis LTM revenue growth | 44.33% | 6.63% direct-peer median | +37.70pp | Nu merits some growth premium, but this does not prove today's full valuation. |
| Current price vs peer NTM-P/E implied value | US$14.30 | US$7.38 | +93.8% to peer-implied value | Mature-bank peers do not support the current price on the chosen forward earnings. |
| NTM P/E vs short own history | 14.8x | 19.4x seven-observation mean | -23.7% | Directional de-rating only; 17 months is too short to establish normal value. |
| FY2025 ROE | 30.3% | Not proven on a matched peer basis | Not assessable | High return weakens simple peer convergence, but covers only two profitable growth years and not a full credit cycle. |

Three explanations for the gap remain:

1. **True mispricing:** the market may be extrapolating exceptional growth and returns too far.
2. **Cycle/rate explanation:** a group cost of equity near 9.78% can reconcile the price; 16.51% is not a group rate.
3. **Quality discount/premium:** Nu's growth deserves a premium, but incomplete cohort economics, credit cyclicality, single-segment disclosure and minority-rights weakness limit how much is proven.

Margin of safety—`(base fair value − price) ÷ base fair value`—is **-121.0201%** using the rounded US$6.47 base and US$14.30 price; the valuation module reports **-121.2%** using its unrounded values. This is distinct from the **69.2308%** loss to the US$4.40 bear value.

## 8. Scenario Model

The valuation module supplied the bull/base/bear levels. The synthesizer adds one **consensus_reconciliation_tail** because the source distribution otherwise fails the span test: the mean sell-side target is US$18.78, and a group cost of equity near 9.78% can reconcile the market price. This tail is disconfirmation, not an engine fair value.

| Case | Probability | Probability basis | Return | Price Target | What Must Happen |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| consensus_reconciliation_tail | 10% | judgment | +31.328671% | US$18.78 | A defensible group cost of equity is nearer 9.78% than 16.51%, and earnings/credit evidence supports the sell-side target. |
| bull | 20% | judgment | -41.048951% | US$8.43 | Forward tangible book and justified P/TBV reach the valuation module's bull inputs. |
| base | 40% | judgment | -54.755245% | US$6.47 | Peer NTM P/E and residual income remain the balanced valuation anchors. |
| bear | 30% | judgment | -69.230769% | US$4.40 | Lower tangible book and/or credit losses justify the 1.20x forward-P/TBV bear. |

**Span check:** the US$18.78 tail is +31.3%, comfortably outside an ordinary weekly move and above the current price. **Conjunction check:** the tail requires both a lower warranted group discount rate and durable earnings/credit. They are not independent—better durable returns are one reason investors may accept a lower hurdle—but the 10% weight is judgment on the joint path, not a product of invented independent probabilities.

The common drivers are the **group cost of equity and the durability of credit returns**. The cases are correlated, not diversified draws. A worse credit cycle can lower tangible book, reduce justified P/TBV and raise the required return at the same time.

- Probability-weighted target price: **US$7.472**.
- Probability-weighted expected return: **-47.7483%**.
- Main upside driver: group cost of equity nearer 9.78%, supported by sustained growth and credit quality.
- Main downside driver: current price above all engine values while credit losses reset returns.
- Risk/reward: **-0.6897x**.
- Verdict: the expected return is not worth the risk for a long. It is also not a short recommendation because the positive tail, borrow, and options evidence are unresolved.

## 9b. Governance & Stewardship

The management-governance **Non-Negotiable Gate is PASS**. Coverage was 114/179, or 63.7%: 31 Green, 77 Amber, 6 Red, 47 Insufficient Data and 18 Not Applicable. Governance Score was 57/100; confidence-adjusted score 39/100; module rating Watchlist; evidence confidence 68/100. [analyses/NU_2026-08-31/management-governance/99_management-governance-synthesis.md, §§1–6, 2026-08-31].

The main issue is control. Founder David Vélez held 18.6% economic ownership and 74.4% voting power through 20-for-1 Class B shares while serving as CEO and chair. This is entrenched control, **not evidence of misconduct**. CIQ reports 22.8% total insider ownership and trailing open-market activity of zero buys/four sales, net -592,707 shares; motive is not proven. [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_20-F(Apr-08-2026).pdf, FY2025, Items 6A, 7A and 10B]; [data/NU/Nu Holdings Ltd NYSE NU Public Ownership Detailed.xls, Capital IQ Insider Trading, through 2026-08-26].

All 24 people were graded Clean on their own reviewed records, but 18 entity branches were not expanded. A coverage-limited network is not a clean network. The single High governance flag is **RF-AUD-007**: KPMG Brazil was censured and fined US$700,000 by the PCAOB for audits of another issuer; Nu was not named. Nu's FY23–FY25 opinions were clean and FY25 internal control over financial reporting was effective, so this is High, non-gate audit-firm risk—not a finding against Nu's accounts. [PCAOB Release 105-2025-008, 2025-03-11]; [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_20-F(Apr-08-2026).pdf, FY2025, Auditor Report and Item 15].

The disclosed legal-exposure build is **US$54.018m = US$44.343m provision + US$9.675m quantified possible claims**. The COP9.3tn GMF all-defendant claim has no Nu allocation and is not added to that total. [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_Interim_Report(Aug-14-2026).pdf, H1 2026, Note 25, pp.32–33]; [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_20-F(Apr-08-2026).pdf, FY2025, Item 8A].

The strongest argument against Avoid is that Nu is not a mature bank: its growth and returns may justify a premium, and a group cost of equity near 9.78% makes the price coherent. The single evidence item that would move the verdict most is a defensible group-wide discount-rate build supported by continued, cash-backed credit returns.

## 10. What Would Kill the Thesis?

The top five things that would make **Avoid** wrong are:

1. A defensible group cost of equity at or below 9.78% on a matched group-wide, post-tax USD basis.
2. A Q3 material dual beat—revenue above US$6.11484bn and EPS above US$0.23272—with no same-period credit deterioration.
3. Two consecutive standalone quarters materially beat both revenue and EPS while delinquency, credit cost and ECL coverage remain stable or improve year over year.
4. A matched direct-peer set shows Nu's current roughly 3.90x FY2027 P/TBV is justified by comparable forward ROE, growth and credit risk.
5. The price falls to or below US$6.47 while the base fair value and prudential evidence remain intact; Avoid would then need a fresh valuation, not automatic continuation.

None of these triggers is already satisfied. The Q3 numeric tests are like-for-like standalone-quarter tests; the model-input and price tests are explicitly labeled non-periodic rather than disguised as operating year-over-year comparisons.

## 11. Positioning and Trade Construction

- **Position:** wait; no long and no short.
- **Entry style:** reconsider only after a fresh valuation. A price near or below US$6.47 is not an automatic buy if fair value falls too.
- **Add levels:** not applicable without an existing position.
- **Stop-loss logic:** not applicable to an Avoid. If an investor nevertheless owns NU, an earnings stop may not protect against a gap.
- **What not to do:** do not turn a negative long return into an automatic short; borrow availability, recall risk and options pricing are absent.
- **Hedge:** no hedge is specified because no position is recommended.
- **Options:** not assessable from available data.

## 12. 2nd Best Bet

No credible second-best bet exists from the available data. The competitive-intel module had zero usable peer calls, so naming Itaú, Bradesco or Santander Brasil as a cleaner expression would outrun the evidence.

## 13. Thesis → Antithesis Iteration

### Thesis 1

Nu's growth and improving risk-adjusted NIM support continued earnings compounding.

### Antithesis 1

The Q3 bar already embeds high growth; much of the sequential NIM gain came from credit income and lower credit cost before the full loss outcome is known.

### Revised Thesis 2

The business can keep growing, but earnings quality and credit durability do not justify treating Q2 as a normalized base.

### Antithesis 2

The engine's valuation may overstate downside because its 16.51% discount rate is not group-wide, and the market price reconciles at 9.78%.

### Final Thesis

Avoid at US$14.30 because the valuation gap survives a broad engine scenario set, but do not short because the discount-rate uncertainty and US$18.78 positive tail are real.

Insight threshold reached: the remaining uncertainty is mostly data-dependent, not reasoning-dependent.

## 14. Math Validation

- Sum of scenario probabilities: **10% + 20% + 40% + 30% = 100%**.
- Probability-weighted expected return: **(10% × 31.328671%) + (20% × -41.048951%) + (40% × -54.755245%) + (30% × -69.230769%) = -47.7483%**.
- Probability-weighted target price: **(10% × US$18.78) + (20% × US$8.43) + (40% × US$6.47) + (30% × US$4.40) = US$7.472**.
- Target-price reconciliation: **(US$7.472 − US$14.30) ÷ US$14.30 = -47.7483%**.
- Risk/reward: **(US$7.472 − US$14.30) ÷ (US$14.30 − US$4.40) = -0.6897x**.
- Downside risk: **−min(+31.328671%, -41.048951%, -54.755245%, -69.230769%) = 69.2308%**.
- Margin of safety on rounded levels: **(US$6.47 − US$14.30) ÷ US$6.47 = -121.0201%**.

The result is most sensitive to the group cost of equity. That is why the distribution includes the US$18.78 reconciliation tail and conviction is downgraded for a single-variable valuation dependency.

Unit economics are partial, not complete: monthly ARPAC of US$17.1 less US$1 cost to serve gives US$16.1 before funding cost, expected credit loss, acquisition cost and capital. It is not a contribution margin. No disqualifier fired and no §24 rejector cap applies.

## Chapter B: Earnings

Source: [analyses/NU_2026-08-31/earnings/99_earnings-synthesis.md, full synthesis, 2026-08-30].

**Verdict: Mixed earnings setup; favors miss.** Earnings clarity was 68/100, earnings quality 54/100 with Material concerns, consensus setup 35/100, earnings volatility 68/100 *(higher is worse)*, data quality 80/100, and synthesis usefulness 65/100 after the unresolved filing-versus-vendor CFO conflict.

Q2 revenue and diluted EPS grew 50.3% and 66.3%, but FY2025 annual revenue growth slowed to 37.0% from 43.4% in FY2024. Credit-card and loan interest added US$1.320bn and supplied 71.6% of Q2 revenue growth. [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_Interim_Report(Aug-14-2026).pdf, Q2/H1 2026, p.5 and Note 6 pp.14–15]; [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_20-F(Apr-08-2026).pdf, FY2025, pp.F-6–F-7].

The Q2 risk-adjusted-NIM bridge reconciles: **+178bp credit income +115bp lower credit cost +5bp float −5bp funding +1bp residual = +294bp**, taking the company-defined measure to 12.4%. Credit income supplied 60.5% of the move. The contradicting series is the implied credit-cost rate, 10.5% versus 8.9% a year earlier. Management's efficiency ratio improved to 19.5% from 21.3%, while the different-basis IFRS opex/revenue ratio worsened to 20.1% from 18.2%. [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_Preliminary_Interim_Report(Aug-13-2026).pdf, Q2 2026, slides 15–16 and 22]; [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_Interim_Report(Aug-14-2026).pdf, Q2 2026, p.5].

H1 CFO was US$(1.242)bn. Filing-built LTM CFO is US$(1.382)bn; Capital IQ reports US$(10.305)bn. The US$8.923bn gap is unresolved, and the reviewed filing wins under the source hierarchy. Bank CFO includes lending, securities and deposit flows, so the figure is not a generic industrial cash-conversion ratio. [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_Interim_Report(Aug-14-2026).pdf, H1 2026, p.12]; [data/NU/Filings/Nu_Holdings_Ltd_-_Form_20-F(Apr-08-2026).pdf, FY2025, pp.F-14–F-15]; [data/NU/ciq_facts.json, ltm_ocf_m, read 2026-08-30].

The FQ3 consensus bar is US$5.93674bn revenue and US$0.22164 GAAP EPS. Material beat markers are US$6.11484bn and US$0.23272; material miss markers are US$5.75864bn and US$0.21056. The four-quarter surprise record is too small for an empirical probability, so the miss weighting is judgment. [data/NU/NuHoldingsLtdNYSENUEstimatesReport.xls, Capital IQ Estimates, Consensus/Surprise/Trends/Revisions, export 2026-08-29].

Five High findings converge on one credit-cycle problem: spread durability, a raised bar, cash/accrual divergence, tax quality and asymmetric macro allowance sensitivity. The US$504.700m downside-macro ECL increase is a pre-tax allowance bound, not an EPS forecast. `RF-EQ-001` is a lender-specific rising-accrual/cash-divergence signal and not proof of misstatement.

## Chapter C: Balance Sheet Survival

Source: [analyses/NU_2026-08-31/balance-sheet-survival/00_solvency-data-triage.md, full triage, 2026-08-30].

**Intentional fail-fast — Insufficient data.** Nu is a regulated bank/lender. The corporate debt/EBITDA, revolver and 40–60% EBITDA stress framework would be invalid. The triage found recent financial statements, debt detail, cash flow, interest, maturity information, leases, contingencies, S&P information and disclosure of no restrictive financial covenants, but not the complete bank-specific evidence required to judge survival.

Missing inputs include group/perimeter CET1, Tier 1 and total capital; risk-weighted assets; regulatory minima and buffers; liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) and net stable funding ratio (NSFR); asset-quality and provisioning returns; committed facility availability; and a bank-appropriate downside stress. The corporate module therefore produced **no Distress, Stretched or Fortress verdict** and no covenant breakpoint.

A mechanical strict net-cash build of **US$7,744.6m = US$13,551.6m cash − US$4,682.3m borrowings − US$1,058.3m repos − US$66.4m leases** is not a bank survival verdict because deposits, regulatory restrictions and liquidity requirements are not reconciled. The nearest vendor maturity is US$1.864bn on 1 June 2027; it is a monitoring event, not proof of distress. [data/NU/ciq_facts.json, debt_maturity_wall, read 2026-08-30].

The module's highest-value next item is the latest primary-regulator prudential return for every regulated perimeter, showing capital ratios, RWA, liquidity, asset quality and provisioning on the regulator's basis. Until then, conviction is capped at 65.

No `RF-MGT-005`, `RF-DISC-001`, `RF-REG-002`, `RF-CAP-004` or `RF-OWN-004` fired. The six §24 filters therefore do not impose a governance cap.

## Chapter G: Valuation

Source: [analyses/NU_2026-08-31/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md, full synthesis, 2026-08-31].

**Verdict: Materially overvalued.** Valuation attractiveness was 5/100, margin-of-safety score 0/100, valuation confidence 48/100, downside risk 90/100 *(higher is worse)*, data quality 80/100 and usefulness 72/100.

The decision line is `NU · NYSE · USD`, with a pool-verified US$14.30 last close on 29 August 2026. Twelve-month bull/base/bear values are US$8.43/US$6.47/US$4.40. The base is 54.8% below price; even the bull is 41.0% below. The full valuation field is US$2.95–US$7.92, a 168% spread. Weighted methods are US$7.38 peer NTM P/E and US$5.55 residual income, 33% apart. Forward P/TBV supplies scenario levels; own-history reversion gets no value because seven observations over 17 months do not establish a cycle-neutral anchor.

The reverse-DCF is conditional. At a 16.51% cost of equity, price implies 47.36% terminal ROE or 80.89% FY2027–30 profit CAGR. But 16.51% is a Brazil Investments CGU rate; the same modeled earnings path reconciles at a 9.78% group-implied rate. That unresolved rate is the single killer risk to the Avoid.

# Business Model Reality Check — NU (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Nu is a digital bank for consumers and small businesses in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia. Its sole reportable segment earns from cards, loans, cash, and investments; interest and gains supplied 85.2% of FY2025 revenue. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, pp.13–15; Item 5, pp.157–158; Note 34, F-97] Reach is the clearest positive: Q2 2026 had 139 million customers and 83.5% activity. [Q2 2026 earnings presentation, slide 6] The main weakness is concentration and incomplete economics: Brazil supplied 91.3% of FY2025 geographic revenue, while cohort contribution and payback are undisclosed. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, F-97; Item 5, p.157] No disqualifier fired. [Disqualifier Scan — NU, Verdict-Lock Signal, 2026-08-30] This average business merits deeper work only with a clear price buffer.

## 1. First-Pass Verdict

### Automatic Disqualifier Check

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Auditor qualification or going-concern note (last 3 years) | N | KPMG gave an unqualified opinion and reported effective internal control; no going-concern note was stated. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm, F-2] |
| 2 | >50% promoter / insider shares pledged | N | The pledged-share numerator is not disclosed, so the ratio is not assessable rather than 0%; no hard trigger is proven. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 7.A, Major Shareholders] |
| 3 | Related-party transactions >25% of revenue or expenses | N | Related-party sales and purchases are not disclosed, so both threshold ratios are not assessable; the disclosed US$0.926m liability is not a revenue or expense numerator. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 28, Related parties] |
| 4 | Auditor changed twice in last 3 years without disclosed reason | N | KPMG audited FY2023–FY2025, implying 0 changes over the test period. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 16.C; FY2024 Form 20-F, Item 16.C] |
| 5 | Material restatement (>5% of revenue or net income) in last 2 years | N | NU reported no error correction or accounting restatement; the FY2024 SAB 122 change was an accounting-policy adoption, not an error correction. [FY2025 Form 20-F, cover disclosure and Item 6.F; FY2024 Form 20-F, auditor report—Crypto Assets] |

CIQ's negative US$10,304.8m LTM read to June 2026 is a later rolling vendor period and is not comparable to this annual test. ### Verdict

- **Verdict:** Average business — worth deeper work only if valuation is cheap

- Business clarity /100: **72** — synthesis judgment: the income engine and sole segment are clear, but product- and country-level profit are not disclosed. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.157–158; Note 34, F-97–F-98]
- Business quality /100: **52** [Business Quality — NU, Aggregate Quality Score, 2026-08-30]
- Moat /100: **65** — the strongest moat-source score is the cost advantage; the moat verdict itself remains narrow and provisional. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5.A, p.157; Moat — NU, Moat Sources and Moat Verdict, 2026-08-30]
- External dependency risk /100 *(higher = worse)*: **59** [External Dependency Check — NU, External Dependency Risk Score, 2026-08-30]

- Overall usefulness /100: **68** — synthesis judgment: the evidence supports a valuation-gated deeper review, but it does not prove full customer-level value creation or a through-cycle moat.

No rejector-filter cap applies. Filter 1—crooks/integrity did not trip because the disqualifier scan emitted no proven integrity trigger. Filter 4—serial acquirers did not trip because acquisition-pattern severity was 28, below 70. Filter 5—fast-changing industry did not trip because the rate-of-change score was 50, above the ≤40 threshold. [Disqualifier Scan — NU, Verdict-Lock Signal, 2026-08-30; Capital Allocation & Governance — NU, Signal Table, 2026-08-30; Business Quality — NU, Quality Factor Table, 2026-08-30]

No capital-structure transaction cap applies. Shares rose 0.8% in FY2025 and then fell 0.5% by June 2026, far below the >25% trigger, and the capital-allocation specialist did not report a >50% year-on-year debt change. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 31, F-84–F-86; Q2 2026 interim financial statements, Note 31, pp.37–39; Capital Allocation & Governance — NU, 2026-08-30]

### Module Disconfirmation

- **Strongest bear point:** Brazil supplied 91.3% of FY2025 geographic revenue, leaving the group exposed to one country's consumer-credit, policy, rate, and currency conditions. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, F-97; Item 3.D, country-risk factors]
- **Strongest bull point:** NU had 139 million customers, an 83.5% activity rate, and US$17 monthly ARPAC—average revenue per active customer—in Q2 2026, evidence of reach and repeat use even though revenue is not contracted. [Q2 2026 earnings presentation, slide 6]
- **Single killer risk:** A weaker Brazilian credit cycle that raises expected credit loss while funding costs stay high would hit the dominant revenue base; the filing does not quantify that combined scenario. [FY2025 Form 20-F, pp.131–132, 166–171]
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** Q2 2026 NIM—net interest income relative to interest-earning assets—rose to 22.9% from 18.8% a year earlier, risk-adjusted NIM rose to 12.4% from 9.9%, and both delinquency measures improved sequentially. These recent readings argue against an immediate deterioration call, but they do not establish through-cycle economics. [Q2 2026 earnings presentation, slides 15, 17–19]

## 3. Reconciliation

- **Revenue basis:** Segment Map uses US$15.775bn of consolidated IFRS revenue, while Customer and Geography Map uses the US$12.084bn geographic-revenue subtotal defined in Note 34. The latter excludes financial expenses and expected credit loss from the consolidated presentation, so geographic shares apply only to that narrower subtotal; they are not segment shares. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Income Statement, F-7; Note 34, F-97–F-98]
- **Brazil share:** Customer and Geography Map reports 91.3%, External Dependency rounds the same filing inputs to 91.4%, and CIQ displays 91%. The synthesis uses the filing's exact US$11,038.313m divided by US$12,083.766m, or 91.3% to one decimal; CIQ's whole-number display is a reconciled vendor rounding, not a separate fact. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, F-97; CIQ Financials→Segments, Geographic Segment → Revenues, FY2025 — vendor export]
- **Moat trajectory:** Moat calls the trajectory provisionally widening, while its own table shows gross margin down 150 basis points. The reconciled read keeps the qualifier: operating leverage and ARPAC improved, but pricing power and market-share widening are not proven; Business Quality's mixed verdict therefore stands. [FY2025 Form 20-F, p.155; Item 5.A, pp.158–159; Moat — NU, Moat Trajectory, 2026-08-30]
- **Operating cash flow:** The audited FY2025 filing reports positive US$3.500bn cash from operations, while CIQ reports negative US$10.305bn for LTM June 2026. Different periods and vendor classification make them unsuitable for direct comparison. The audited annual series governs the four-year disqualifier test; the later LTM vendor read remains unreconciled and must not be relabelled as a filing figure. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Cash Flows, F-14; CIQ Financials→Cash Flow, “Cash from Ops.”, LTM June 2026 — vendor export]

No material disagreement remains after preserving these period, scope, source, and definition differences.

## 4. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- **Strongest business-model positive:** Scale is paired with frequent use: Q2 2026 had 139 million customers, 83.5% activity, and US$17 monthly ARPAC. [Q2 2026 earnings presentation, slide 6]
- **Strongest business-model negative:** Brazil supplied 91.3% of FY2025 geographic revenue, so country-specific credit, rate, policy, regulatory, and FX shocks can affect most of the measured revenue base at once. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, F-97; Item 3.D, country-risk factors]
- **Most important segment:** Nu Group is the sole reportable segment and supplies 100% of disclosed segment revenue and profit; Brazil is the economic concentration, not a separately reported segment. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, F-97–F-98]
- **Cleanest unit-economics read:** US$17.1 monthly ARPAC less US$1.0 cost to serve equals US$16.1 per active customer, but this is revenue minus partial service cost, not contribution margin, because financial-service costs and expected credit loss are excluded. [Q2 2026 earnings presentation, slide 28; FY2025 Form 20-F, p.171]
- **Versus named peers:** NU's four-year IFRS ROE—net income earned on average shareholder capital—was 17.2%, between Itaú's 24.3% and Santander Brasil's 12.5% and near Bradesco's 16.2%. The peer figures are current management-defined measures, so no precise ranking is supported; matched gross and EBIT margins are unavailable. [FY2025 Form 20-F, pp.155, 157; Itaú 2Q26 Form 6-K; Bradesco 2Q26 Form 6-K, p.7; Santander Brasil 2Q26 Form 6-K, p.3]
- **Main external dependency:** Brazilian consumer-credit conditions, followed by interest rates and regulation; specified hedges do not remove household-demand or default risk. [FY2025 Form 20-F, pp.53, 131–132, 166–167; H1 2026 interim financial statements, Notes 20 and 32]
- **Capital allocation and governance:** Audit history is clean and no serial-acquirer pattern is proven, but David Vélez's 74.4% voting power gives the founder/CEO/chair decisive control over outside Class A holders. [FY2025 Form 20-F, pp.193, 203]
- **Contingent credit exposure:** US$38.164bn of unused card limits was off balance sheet but included in expected-credit-loss measurement; it is a disclosed lending commitment, not an undisclosed financing vehicle. [Q2 2026 interim financial statements, Note 32, p.40]
- **Automatic disqualifier:** None triggered. Pledged shares and related-party sales/purchases remain not assessable rather than zero. [Disqualifier Scan — NU, Disqualifier Check, 2026-08-30]
- **Rejector filters and caps:** Crooks/integrity, serial acquirers, and fast-changing industry did not trip. No rejector-filter cap or capital-structure transaction cap was applied. [Disqualifier Scan — NU, 2026-08-30; Capital Allocation & Governance — NU, 2026-08-30; Business Quality — NU, 2026-08-30]
- **Deferred-tax flag:** The US$991.046m H1 2026 deferred-tax benefit was 51.3% of US$1.933bn net income, and the US$3.649bn net deferred-tax asset was 27.5% of equity. Future taxable profit must support realization; the filing's support means this is estimate dependence, not evidence of improper accounting. [Q2 2026 interim financial statements, pp.7–8; Note 30, pp.36–37]
- **Legal and tax provision flag:** The provision balance rose US$13.423m, or 43.4%, in six months to US$44.343m, with H1 additions of US$27.370m versus US$14.474m a year earlier. The balance is small beside group earnings, but the direction is adverse and cash timing is uncertain. [Q2 2026 interim financial statements, Note 25, pp.32–33; Cash Flows, p.12]
- **Biggest missing data point:** A new-customer cohort table showing revenue, funding cost, expected credit loss, full variable cost, retention, lifetime contribution, and payback. Without it, NU's low CAC and high ARPAC do not prove that each new customer creates value. [FY2025 Form 20-F, p.157; Q2 2026 earnings presentation, slide 28]
- **Deeper-work decision:** Yes, but only as a valuation-gated average business. A full cohort-profit disclosure and IFRS ROE staying above a group-relevant cost of equity through a weaker credit period would move the answer toward high quality; FY2026 IFRS ROE below that hurdle, failed deferred-tax-asset realization, or credit losses overwhelming the improved spread would move it toward low quality. [Moat — NU, Economic Moat Test and Moat Verdict, 2026-08-30; Q2 2026 interim financial statements, Note 30, pp.36–37]

## 5. Simple Summary

- Nu is a mobile-first retail bank for consumers and small businesses in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, pp.13–15]
- Interest and financial-instrument gains supplied 85.2% of FY2025 revenue; card and partner fees supplied the rest. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.157–158]
- NU has not shown whether each new customer creates value: ARPAC is revenue, and cost to serve excludes funding cost and credit loss. [Q2 2026 earnings presentation, slide 28; FY2025 Form 20-F, p.171]
- The group reports one segment. Brazil supplied 91.3% of the narrower FY2025 geographic-revenue subtotal. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, F-97–F-98]
- The moat is narrow and only provisionally widening, built mainly on low-cost digital distribution and scale rather than network effects; Itaú, Bradesco, and Santander Brasil remain powerful named competitors. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D; Item 5.A, p.157]
- Rates, regulation, and the Brazilian consumer-credit cycle matter more than commodities or industrial demand. [FY2025 Form 20-F, pp.53, 131–132, 166–167]
- Capital allocation has no proven serial-acquirer pattern, but the founder/CEO/chair controls 74.4% of the vote. [FY2025 Form 20-F, pp.193, 203]
- No automatic disqualifier fired. NU deserves deeper work only if valuation compensates for Brazil concentration, incomplete cohort economics, and estimate-heavy H1 tax benefits.

## business-model / 02_business-identity.md

_Source: `business-model/02_business-identity.md`_

# Business Identity — NU

## 1. What The Company Actually Does

Nu is a mobile-first financial-services group that offers accounts, credit and prepaid cards, consumer and small-business lending, payments, savings and investment products, and insurance distribution through one app for individual consumers and small businesses in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, pp.13–15]
Customers use Nu to pay, hold and move money, borrow, save, invest, and buy protection without using a branch; merchants and financial-product partners are also part of the payment and distribution flows. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, pp.14, 32–35; p.158]
*Inference, not from filings:* its economic engine is balance-sheet-led rather than a software subscription model: interest income and gains on financial instruments were 85.2% of FY2025 revenue, generated chiefly from card receivables, loans, and cash/investment assets. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, p.157]
Customer deposits support its funding needs; *inference, not from filings:* this makes deposit pricing, credit quality, and the size and mix of the credit book important alongside customer growth. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, p.157]
Nu also makes fee income when customers use its cards and through loyalty subscriptions, late fees, and partner commissions for investments, insurance, remittances, and marketplace sales. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, p.158]
At Q2 2026, management reported 139 million customers, an 83.5% activity rate, and US$17 monthly ARPAC (average revenue per active customer); these are management measures, with ARPAC defined as monthly revenue divided by average monthly active customers. [Q2 2026 earnings-call transcript, prepared remarks, pp.4–5; Q2’26 earnings deck, slide 6]

## 2. How The Company Makes Money

**Core financial income:**

`Interest and gains = (interest-bearing credit-card receivables + customer loans + cash/investment assets) × yield, plus/minus financial-instrument gains and losses`

Nu charges interest on revolving and refinanced card balances, purchased card receivables, and customer loans; it also earns interest and records gains or losses on its financial assets. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.157, 169]

**Fee income:**

`Fee and commission income = card purchase volume × interchange rate (net of rewards) + subscription fees + late fees + partner and marketplace commissions`

Most fee income comes from credit and prepaid-card transactions. Mastercard-set interchange varies by merchant segment and is paid by accepting merchants, while Nu also earns the other fee streams shown in the formula. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.158, 169–170]

*Inference, grounded in the disclosed revenue streams:* volume is driven by customer acquisition, active use, card purchase volume, lending balances, deposits, and adoption of more products by existing customers. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.157–158, 175]
*Inference, grounded in the disclosed revenue streams:* price is driven mainly by lending yields, the market rates earned on cash and investment assets, interchange, and paid tiers; interest-rate changes can affect both earned yields and funding costs. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.157–158]
*Inference, grounded in the disclosed cost structure:* margin depends on the spread after deposit and other funding costs, expected credit loss (ECL), payment-network and chargeback costs, rewards, and customer-service/operating costs. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.157, 170]

## 3. Business Type Classification

*Inference, not from filings:* Latin American digital retail bank/lender, using customer deposits to support funding needs and earning card-payment and distribution fees alongside interest income. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.157–158]

## 3a. Sector Overlay & Required-KPI Checklist

*Inference, not from filings:* the **bank / lender** overlay applies because lending and deposit-funded net interest income dominate NU’s revenue model. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.157–158; SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md, Bank / lender row]

| Required KPI | Status in data pool | Evidence / data gap |
|---|---|---|
| Net interest margin (NIM) | Present | The Q2 2026 deck reports NIM and risk-adjusted NIM and defines both. [Q2’26 earnings deck, slides 15–16, 38] |
| Loan and deposit growth | Present | The FY2025 filing reports deposits and an interest-earning portfolio, while the Q2 deck tracks the credit portfolio and deposits. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, p.12; Q2’26 earnings deck, slides 13–14] |
| CASA / funding mix | Absent | The pool reports total deposits and their cost, but does not report a standard CASA split. Do not substitute the reported deposit balance or cost of deposits for CASA. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, p.157; Q2’26 earnings deck, slide 14] |
| GNPA, NNPA / NPL | Present for NPL; GNPA/NNPA labels not used | The deck reports 15–90-day and 90+-day NPL ratios across the credit portfolio; these are the relevant delinquency measures, not Indian GNPA/NNPA labels. [Q2’26 earnings deck, slide 17] |
| Credit cost (provisions / loans) | Present | The deck reports credit cost and defines risk-adjusted NIM as NII net of credit-loss allowance over interest-earning assets. [Q2’26 earnings deck, slides 15–16, 38] |
| PCR (coverage) | Present | It reports credit-loss-allowance coverage over the 90+-day NPL stock. [Q2’26 earnings deck, slide 19] |
| CET1 / CAR | Present for CAR | The FY2025 filing reports regulatory capital ratios for the Brazilian, Mexican, and Colombian regulated entities. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 36—Capital Management, pp.236–238] |
| ROA | Absent | No group ROA was located in the current primary financial releases; ROE must not be used as a substitute. [Q2’26 earnings deck, slide 23] |
| ROE | Present | The Q2 2026 deck reports annualized, non-GAAP ROE. [Q2’26 earnings deck, slide 23] |
| Cost-to-income | Absent on the strict basis | The deck reports an efficiency ratio with a different stated denominator, not a standard cost-to-income ratio. [Q2’26 earnings deck, slides 6, 22, 37] |

The overlay’s red flags are rapid unseasoned loan growth, rising NPLs with falling coverage, NIM supported by riskier mix, restructuring/evergreening, and related-party lending. Its valuation norm is dividend-discount or residual-income analysis using the cost of equity, with price-to-book assessed against ROE; FCFF/EV is not the primary method. [SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md, Bank / lender row]

## 4. What Drives Variance

*Inference, grounded in the disclosed revenue and cost definitions:* revenue normally moves with customer activity, card purchase volume, credit balances, loan growth, deposits and the yield earned on assets; in FY2025 the company attributed revenue growth chiefly to card and loan interest income and to card-income growth with purchase volume. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, p.175]
*Inference, grounded in disclosed revenue and cost definitions:* interest rates and credit/product mix change both lending and float income, while interchange and paid tiers affect fees; the same rate environment can raise deposit funding costs and affect borrowers’ ability to repay. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, pp.157–158]
*Inference, grounded in the disclosed cost definitions:* margins move with funding expense, ECL, payment-network and chargeback costs, rewards, and operating cost; FX can also change the U.S.-dollar presentation, so the Q2 deck’s FX-neutral comparisons should not be confused with reported IFRS results. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5, p.170; Q2 2026 earnings-call transcript, prepared remarks, p.4]

# Segment Map — NU

## 1. Segment Table

Basis: FY2025 ended 31 December 2025. Nu reports under IFRS Accounting Standards in U.S. dollars. [^0]

| Segment | What It Does | Revenue Share | Profit Share | Margin Quality | Capital Intensity | Cyclicality | Main Risk |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Nu Group (the single reportable segment) | Digital retail financial services: credit-card and loan interest, plus card, insurance, and other fee income. [^2] | 100% (US$15.775bn total revenue) [^1] | 100% (US$2.872bn IFRS net income; no separate segment-profit measure) [^1] | Not disclosed — Nu provides no segment EBIT or segment margin. [^1] | High — US$21.751bn of credit-card receivables plus US$10.915bn of gross loans, or US$32.667bn before expected-credit-loss allowances; regulated subsidiaries also require capital. [^3] | Mid — interest rates directly affect interest income, funding costs and borrower defaults. [^4] | Credit losses, funding costs and regulatory-capital needs. [^3][^4] |

## 2. Dominant Segment

Nu is effectively a single-segment business: its CEO, the chief operating decision maker, allocates capital and reviews performance for the whole Group on a consolidated basis, so the Group represents 100% of disclosed revenue and profit. [^1] Brazil is the economic concentration, but not a separately reported profit segment: the geographical disclosure records US$11.038bn (91%) of its defined revenue in Brazil, US$0.808bn (7%) in Mexico and US$0.237bn (2%) in other countries, with no country profit disclosed. [^5] Those geographical figures are not a substitute for reportable-segment shares because the table's US$12.084bn revenue total has a narrower product scope than consolidated IFRS total revenue of US$15.775bn. [^1][^5]

## 3. Segment Disclosure Quality

The single-segment definition is consistent across the FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 20-F filings; there is no reportable “Other” or corporate segment, and no product- or geography-level profit or EBIT measure. [^6] The current filing does disclose product categories in Note 6 and geography in Note 34, but the latter reports only defined revenue and non-current assets, not country profit; its “Other countries” line is 2% of the geographic revenue subtotal, not an “Other” business segment. [^2][^5] Management’s Q2 2026 commentary continues to describe Brazil, Mexico and Colombia as three core markets, but it does not create reportable country segments or provide country profit. [^7] Capital IQ’s latest annual business-segment export labels the sole business line “Banking” at US$6.991bn (100%); it reconciles exactly to the audited US$15.775bn total revenue less US$4.579bn interest and other financial expenses and US$4.205bn expected credit loss: US$15.775bn − US$4.579bn − US$4.205bn = US$6.991bn. This is a vendor presentation of the one consolidated business, not evidence of a second segment. Its geographic revenue subtotal of US$12.084bn (Brazil US$11.038bn, Mexico US$0.808bn, other countries US$0.237bn) matches the filing’s geographic table; it has no geographic profit measure. [^1][^5][^8]

## business-model / 04_unit-economics.md

_Source: `business-model/04_unit-economics.md`_

# Unit Economics — NU

## 1. Natural Unit

The natural economic unit for Nu Group (the single reportable segment) is an individual monthly active customer. Nu reports under IFRS Accounting Standards in U.S. dollars. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Note 34, F-97; Presentation of Financial and Other Information, p.1]

Secondary units are credit-card and loan exposures and card-payment transactions, but Nu does not disclose product-level contribution economics. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Note 6, F-39]

## 2. Unit Economics Table

| Unit Economic | Value | Period | Direction vs Prior Year (Improving / Stable / Deteriorating / Unknown) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue per unit | US$17.1 monthly ARPAC (average monthly revenue per average individual monthly active customer) | Q2 2026 | Improving: US$13.8 in Q2 2025 and US$15.9 in Q1 2026 | [Nu Holdings Ltd., Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slide 28] |
| Gross margin per unit | Not disclosed. The reported FY2025 gross margin was 42.0% at Group level, not a per-active-customer margin. | FY2025 | Unknown | [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Gross Profit, p.171] |
| Contribution margin per unit (after variable costs) | Not disclosed. The US$1.0 monthly cost to serve is not a contribution-cost measure: it covers transaction, customer-support and operations costs, while financial-service costs and expected credit losses sit outside it. | Q2 2026 | Unknown | [Nu Holdings Ltd., Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slide 28; Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Monthly Average Cost to Serve per Active Customer, p.161; Gross Profit, p.171] |
| Cost to acquire / build the unit | US$7.4 CAC per customer; paid marketing was about 32% of CAC. | FY2025 | Deteriorating: US$6.4 in FY2024 | [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Overview—Low Cost to Acquire, p.157] |
| Payback period or unit lifetime | Not disclosed. Net churn was 0.1% per month, but Nu does not translate that figure into a lifetime or a CAC payback calculation. | FY2025 | Improving: net churn was 0.2% per month in FY2024 | [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Net Churn, p.163] |

## 3. Value Creation Read

**Verdict: Unclear.** The disclosed operating spread is favorable but incomplete: Q2 2026 ARPAC of US$17.1 less the US$1.0 cost to serve equals US$16.1 per active customer per month. That is a revenue-minus-partial-service-cost spread, not contribution margin, because the US$1.0 measure excludes financial-service costs and expected credit losses. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slide 28; Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Gross Profit, p.171]

CAC of US$7.4 per customer is below one month of the current disclosed ARPAC, but the two metrics are from different periods and ARPAC is not profit. Nu therefore has not disclosed the cohort revenue, funding cost, expected credit loss, full variable cost, retention and lifetime contribution needed to test whether contribution margin × lifetime exceeds CAC. The single most valuable missing disclosure is a new-customer cohort table with those inputs and a stated payback period. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Overview—Low Cost to Acquire, p.157; Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slide 28]

## 4. Sensitivity

Expected credit loss is the input most likely to change this read, because it is not included in cost to serve. FY2025 expected credit loss was US$4.2049 billion; a mechanical 20% increase is US$0.8410 billion and, holding revenue and every other cost unchanged, would reduce Group gross profit from US$6.6250 billion to US$5.7840 billion—a 12.7% reduction. This is a zero-mitigation bound, not a forecast or a per-customer result. Expected credit loss rose 32.7% in FY2025 while the reported monthly cost to serve stayed US$0.8 in FY2023–FY2025; the series use different bases, so this does not establish a unit-level causal attribution, but it shows why credit loss matters more than the reported servicing-cost line alone. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Gross Profit, p.171; Monthly Average Cost to Serve per Active Customer, p.161]

| Brazil | 91.3% FY2025; 90.9% H1 2026 | Stable concentration — H1 share eased from 91.9% in 2025 to 90.9% in 2026 | FY2025: US$11,038.313m of US$12,083.766m [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, p. F-97]; H1 2026: US$7,576.852m of US$8,333.266m [Q2 2026 unaudited interim consolidated financial statements, Note 34, p. 43] | A Brazil-specific macroeconomic, regulatory, or currency shock would affect most revenue. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D Risk Factors—Risks Relating to the Countries in Which We Operate] |
| Mexico | 6.7% FY2025; 7.2% H1 2026 | Growing — H1 share rose from 6.0% in 2025 to 7.2% in 2026 | FY2025: US$808.113m [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, p. F-97]; H1 2026: US$603.629m [Q2 2026 unaudited interim consolidated financial statements, Note 34, p. 43] | Revenue mix is still small relative to Brazil. |
| Other countries | 2.0% FY2025; 1.8% H1 2026 | Declining share — H1 share moved from 2.1% in 2025 to 1.8% in 2026 | FY2025: US$237.340m [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, p. F-97]; H1 2026: US$152.785m [Q2 2026 unaudited interim consolidated financial statements, Note 34, p. 43] | The filing does not separately disclose revenue by country within this bucket, so a Colombia-specific revenue share is not assessable. |

## 3. Concentration Flags

| Concentration Flag | Triggered (Y/N) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| One customer >20% of revenue | N | No single customer represented 10% or more of group revenue in FY2023–FY2025 or H1 2026, which rules out a customer above 20%. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, p. F-97] [Q2 2026 unaudited interim consolidated financial statements, Note 34, p. 43] |
| Top 3 customers >40% of revenue | N | Each customer was below 10%; the three largest combined were therefore below 30%, not above 40%, for the disclosed periods. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, p. F-97] |
| One geography >50% of revenue | Y | Brazil supplied 91.3% of FY2025 geographical revenue and 90.9% in H1 2026. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, p. F-97] [Q2 2026 unaudited interim consolidated financial statements, Note 34, p. 43] |
| One customer or geography >30% with no long-term contract disclosed | Y | This is a geography flag, not a named-customer flag: Brazil was 91.3% of FY2025 revenue, while Nu states that it generally does not have long-term customer contracts. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, p. F-97; Item 3.D Risk Factors—customer retention] |

## 4. Read

NU is not customer-concentrated in the disclosed revenue data: no single customer reached 10% of revenue, and the base consists of individual consumers and SMEs rather than a few named accounts. Geography is highly concentrated, however, because Brazil supplied 91.3% of FY2025 revenue and 90.9% of H1 2026 revenue, despite Mexico's share rising to 7.2% in H1 2026. The single biggest dependency is Brazilian economic, regulatory, and currency conditions; this is not protected by long-term customer contracts. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, p. F-97; Item 3.D Risk Factors—Risks Relating to the Countries in Which We Operate]

## business-model / 06_value-chain.md

_Source: `business-model/06_value-chain.md`_

# Value Chain Position — NU

## 1. Stages Occupied

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Service provider — deposit taker and lender | Nu gathers retail deposits and extends consumer and small-business credit through its app, earning interest income, card fees and distribution commissions. | Mid | Mid | Retail deposits were its main funding source: US$41.9bn at 31 December 2025, of which 92.5% was payable on demand; the company can set offered deposit yields, but deposit supply and funding cost depend on customer confidence, competing offers and market rates. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D — Risk Factors: liquidity and retail deposits] |
| Card issuer and payment platform | Nu issues credit and prepaid cards and processes payment activity, but Mastercard authorizes its card transactions and its rules set key operating conditions. | Weak | Mid | Mastercard is a sole or limited-source provider for certain services, can charge transaction fees, and a significant source of Nu revenue comes through its payment scheme; Nu can offer credit and fee products, but network rules and Brazilian interchange caps limit that control. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D — Risk Factors: third-party service providers and Mastercard payment scheme, pp.111–112; Item 4.B — Business Overview] |
| End-customer-facing digital financial-services brand | Nu distributes accounts, savings, investments, insurance and payment products directly to individual consumers and small businesses through one app. | Mid | Mid | It can tailor the price of loans and deposits customer by customer, according to management, but customers can compare and switch providers and the filing says competitors can force higher deposit rates, lower loan rates or lower fees. [Q2 2026 earnings-call transcript, Q&A; FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D — Risk Factors: competition and open finance] |
| Distributor of third-party financial products | Nu earns partner and marketplace commissions when customers use investment, insurance, remittance and marketplace products offered through its app. | Mid | Mid | Partner commissions are a disclosed fee stream, but the pool does not disclose partner terms, exclusivity, or the revenue share of any partner. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5 — Results of Operations, pp.157–158] |

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

**Answer this on two separate axes, and never let one stand in for the other (CLAUDE.md §9).**

| Axis | What it asks | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Contractual pass-through** | Is there an escalator, indexed-pricing, or cost-plus clause that moves price automatically? | **No disclosed automatic pass-through.** No indexed, cost-plus, or automatic customer-price clause was located in the available filings; this is not proof that none exists. The filing says network-rule changes and inflation-related costs may not be passed to customers in every circumstance. | [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D — Risk Factors: Mastercard payment scheme, pp.111–112; Item 3.D — Risk Factors: inflation, p.136] |
| **Realised recovery** | Of a given input-cost increase, how much did the company actually recover — through price, mix, hedging, re-sourcing, or a cost programme? | **Not computable from the pool.** Nu does not disclose a matched gross pre-mitigation input-cost shock and the associated reported margin impact, so the required recovery calculation cannot be made. | [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D — Risk Factors: Mastercard payment scheme and inflation; Q2 2026 earnings-call transcript, prepared remarks] |

Nu has some economic tools, but the pool does not measure their recovery rate. In Q2 2026, management said it was optimizing Mexico deposits, lowering the cost of deposits to 88% of the local interbank rate, three percentage points below a year earlier, while Mexican deposits declined modestly. It also described individualized loan and deposit pricing. These are funding-cost and product-pricing levers, not evidence that Nu passed a specific network, cloud, or inflation cost to customers. In 2025, Nu said changes to Brazilian deposit remuneration and Money Boxes had no material impact on deposit inflows; that is cost absorption through funding-price management, not customer price pass-through. [Q2 2026 earnings-call transcript, prepared remarks and Q&A; FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5 — Key Business Metrics: Deposits]

**Supplier / input concentration (quantify).** The filing does not disclose the largest supplier's share of purchases or COGS, a top-three supplier share, or the cost share of any input. It does, however, identify Mastercard and certain other third-party services as sole-source or limited-source, and says replacement could be difficult and disruptive. Mastercard authorizes Nu's credit and prepaid-card transactions, making it a material operational dependency even though its spend share is not disclosed. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D — Risk Factors: third-party service providers]

## 2A. Named Counterparties

The Capital IQ Suppliers/Customers views cover only recently disclosed relationships (within the last two years) for current subsidiaries; they are not Nu's full supplier or customer base. [CIQ Suppliers/Customers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export]

| Counterparty | Listing | What it supplies / buys | Which group entity | Who disclosed it | Why it matters here |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MasterCard International Incorporated | *unlisted* | Transaction and payment-processing services; supplier and licensor | Nu Holdings Ltd. and Nu BN México / Nu Pagamentos subsidiaries | Nu 2026 Form 20-F | The graph corroborates the filing's payment-network dependency; terms and spend are not disclosed. [CIQ Suppliers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; Nu Holdings Ltd. 2026 Form 20-F] |
| Amazon Web Services, Inc. | *unlisted* | Internet-services and infrastructure supplier | Nu Holdings Ltd. | Nu 2026 Form 20-F | Cloud infrastructure is a named operating input; the graph does not establish spend, exclusivity or switchability. [CIQ Suppliers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; Nu Holdings Ltd. 2026 Form 20-F] |
| Wise Group plc | LSE:WISE | Transaction and payment-processing supplier | Nu Pagamentos S.A. — Instituição de Pagamento | Wise filing | A third-party-disclosed payment-services relationship; it could affect product delivery, but size and contract terms are not disclosed. [CIQ Suppliers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; Wise Group plc — Form Doc] |
| Edenred SE | ENXTPA:EDEN | Transaction and payment-processing supplier | Nu Holdings Ltd. | Edenred filing | A third-party-disclosed payment-services relationship; it supports the view that Nu relies on external payment inputs, not a disclosed dependency percentage. [CIQ Suppliers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; Edenred SE — Form Doc] |
| United States International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) | *unlisted* | Creditor / financing provider | Nu Colombia S.A. | Nu 2026 Form 20-F | This is financing exposure rather than a trade-volume supplier; the graph does not give the loan amount, price or maturity. [CIQ Suppliers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; Nu Holdings Ltd. 2026 Form 20-F] |
| Circle Internet Group, Inc. | NYSE:CRCL | Client services customer relationship | Nu Pagamentos S.A. — Instituição de Pagamento | Circle 2025 Form S-1 | The only named outside customer relationship in the export; the filing source is the counterparty's, and neither side's revenue share is disclosed. [CIQ Customers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; Circle Internet Group 2025 Form S-1] |
| Computershare Trust Company, National Association | *unlisted* | Transfer-agent services | Nu Holdings Ltd. | Nu 2026 Form 20-F | Necessary corporate-service provider but not a core operating input; no size or contract terms are disclosed. [CIQ Suppliers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; Nu Holdings Ltd. 2026 Form 20-F] |
| Numis Corporation Limited | *unlisted* | Investment-banking and brokerage supplier | Nu Holdings Ltd. | Numis filing | A third-party-disclosed advisory/brokerage relationship; no operating dependency is evidenced. [CIQ Suppliers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; Numis Corporation Limited — Form Doc] |
| Mercedes-Benz Grand Prix Limited | *unlisted* | Movies and entertainment supplier | Nu Holdings Ltd. | Key Development / client announcement, 2026-01-21 | The graph names a commercial relationship, but it does not establish a procurement cost or operational reliance. [CIQ Suppliers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; Key DevelopmentClient Announcements, 2026-01-21] |

- **Concentration of disclosure.** The graph identifies nine outside parties, three with listed lines, across the NYSE, LSE and Euronext Paris; none of its 11 relationship rows is intragroup. [CIQ Suppliers/Customers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export]
- **Where the spend clusters.** Three named third parties are in transaction and payment processing (Edenred, Wise and Mastercard); two are in investment banking and brokerage (Computershare and Numis). That shows where disclosed relationships cluster, not how much Nu spends. [CIQ Suppliers/Customers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export]
- **The honest limit.** The export proves named relationships, not the share of Nu's purchases, funding, revenue, or a counterparty's business; it cannot be converted into a dependency percentage. [CIQ Suppliers/Customers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export]

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

Nu has partial, product-level pricing control rather than proven broad customer pricing power. Management says it can set a personalized price for each loan, credit product or deposit offer. The observable 2025–Q2 2026 actions are mainly **upstream funding** decisions: Nu changed deposit remuneration and Money Boxes in Brazil without a material reported effect on deposit inflows in 2025, then optimized Mexican deposits in Q2 2026, with a modest deposit decline and a cost of deposits 3 percentage points lower year on year. Those results do not show that borrowers or merchants accepted a higher Nu price. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5 — Key Business Metrics: Deposits; Q2 2026 earnings-call transcript, prepared remarks and Q&A]

On the downstream side, no specific loan-rate or fee increase and matching volume reaction were located in the last 24 months. The filing instead says Nu could be forced to raise deposit rates, cut loan rates or cut fees when customers receive better competing offers; customers do not have long-term contracts, and open-finance rules make switching easier. Brazilian regulation also caps prepaid-card interchange at 0.7% and debit-card interchange at 0.5%, constraining a key card-payment price. **Not proven from available data** that Nu can raise customer prices without losing volume. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D — Risk Factors: competition and open finance; Item 3.D — Risk Factors: customers; Item 4.B — Brazilian payments regulation]

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.** Nu has meaningful control over product and deposit offers and benefits from a large retail deposit base, but its funding price is set in a contest with customers and market rates. Its card-payment economics are less controlled: Mastercard authorizes transactions, may raise per-transaction fees, and controls rules that Nu may not always pass on; Brazilian interchange caps further restrict price. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D — Risk Factors: liquidity, competition, third-party providers and Mastercard payment scheme, pp.111–112; Item 4.B — Brazilian payments regulation]

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

**Mastercard payment-scheme terms and continuity:** Nu relies on Mastercard for card authorization and a significant source of card-related revenue; fee or rule changes, suspension, or loss of registration could hurt both service continuity and margins, with no disclosed timely substitute. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D — Risk Factors: third-party service providers and Mastercard payment scheme, pp.111–112]

## business-model / 07_business-quality.md

_Source: `business-model/07_business-quality.md`_

# Business Quality — NU

Sector overlay applied: bank / lender — factors Margin stability, Capital intensity, Commodity dependence, and Cyclicality use the sector-specific bank lens.

## 1. Quality Factor Table

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 55 | Brazil caps prepaid-card interchange at 0.7%; payment-scheme rules set interchange by payment type and merchant class. Fee and commission income was 14.8% of FY2025 revenue. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, “Regulation of Credit Cards and Interchange Fees”; Item 5.A, p.158] | Moderate only. Lending yields and risk pricing give Nu some control, but a material payments revenue stream is scheme- and regulation-constrained; a high NIM does not by itself prove durable pricing power. |
| Repeat / recurring revenue *(higher = better)* | 70 | Q2 2026 had 139 million customers, an 83.5% activity rate and US$17 monthly ARPAC (average revenue per active customer). [Q2’26 earnings presentation, slide 6] | Accounts, cards, deposits and credit can create repeat daily revenue. This is recurring financial activity rather than contracted subscription revenue. |
| Customer stickiness *(higher = better)* | 60 | ARPAC rose from US$15.0 in Q1 2025 to US$17.1 in Q2 2026; the disclosed 90-month cohort showed US$30.7 monthly ARPAC. Nu also states that customers generally have no long-term contracts and that deposits may be withdrawn without notice. [Q2’26 earnings presentation, slide 28; FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D, “Our ability to attract and retain customers…”] | Rising cohort monetization and a high activity rate support engagement, but the filing does not supply a retention rate and makes clear that balances and product use are cancellable. |
| Margin stability *(higher = better)* | 58 | Q2 2026 NIM was 22.9% and risk-adjusted NIM was 12.4%, versus 18.8% and 9.9% in Q2 2025; risk-adjusted NIM subtracts credit cost. [Q2’26 earnings presentation, slide 15] | Bank-margin lens applied. The latest spread improved, but the 410-basis-point NIM range from 18.8% to 22.9% over the cited year and credit-cost sensitivity keep this below a stable-margin score. |
| Capital intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 55 | At FY2025, gross credit-card receivables and loans were US$21.751bn and US$10.915bn, respectively; the Brazilian conglomerate had a US$3.3bn minimum regulatory-capital requirement at 31 December 2025. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 13, p.F-50; Note 14, p.F-57; Item 4.B, “Prudential and Capital Requirements”] | Bank-capital lens applied. Deposit funding lowers the cash investment needed to grow, but a larger credit book consumes regulatory capital and cannot scale like a software product. |
| Competitive intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 45 | The filing says regional regulators are promoting initiatives intended to increase efficiency, competition and innovation; it also warns that regulation has made customer switching easier. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, “Favorable Regulatory Environment”; Item 3.D, “Our ability to attract and retain customers…”] | Incumbent-bank concentration is not the same as low competitive pressure. Digital entrants, payment alternatives and easier switching limit the benefit from that concentration. |
| Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk *(low rate-of-change = high score)* | 50 | Nu identifies technological change, increased competition and regulatory change as causes of operating-result fluctuation. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D, “Our results of operations may fluctuate…”] | The underlying need for deposits, payments and credit is durable, but the digital delivery model, instant-payment rails and regulation keep the competitive playbook moving. This is a mixed, not a fast-changing-industry, score. |
| Regulatory dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 35 | Nu’s Brazilian subsidiaries are regulated by the BCB, CVM, CMN and/or SUSEP; capital requirements depend on risk-weighted assets and buffers. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, “Our Regulatory Position”; “Prudential and Capital Requirements”] | Licensing, capital, card rules and conduct requirements directly set the room to offer products and earn returns. This is a core business constraint, not a peripheral compliance cost. |
| Commodity dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 45 | For this bank/lender, the relevant exposure is the rate cycle: the filing flags exchange-rate and interest-rate instability, while the Q2 deposit cost was 87% of the respective interbank rate. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D, “Risks Relating to the Countries in Which We Operate”; Q2’26 earnings presentation, slide 14] | Bank-rate lens applied. Nu is not exposed to a raw-material price, but funding cost and earned asset yield move with local rates and product mix. |
| Cyclicality *(low cyclicality = high score)* | 45 | Q2 2026 15–90-day NPLs were 4.85%, down from 5.02% in Q1, and 90+-day NPLs were 6.5%, down from 6.9%; the same presentation reports risk-adjusted NIM of 12.4%. [Q2’26 earnings presentation, slides 15, 17–19] | Bank-credit-cycle lens applied. The latest delinquency movement was favorable, but loan losses, funding cost and borrower affordability remain tied to the Brazilian and wider Latin American credit cycle. |
| Disclosure quality *(higher = better)* | 68 | Nu provides audited IFRS financial statements and a geographical-revenue note, but reports one operating segment and does not disclose country profit. Brazil was US$11.038bn (91%) of the FY2025 geographical-revenue subtotal, reconciling to the CIQ geographic export’s US$11,038m (91%) read. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, pp.F-97–F-98; CIQ Financials→Segments, Geographic Segment → Revenues, latest annual column — vendor export, retrieved 2026-08-29] | Primary disclosure is usable for revenue, credit assets, capital and geography. Country profitability, a standard CASA split, group ROA and a strict cost-to-income ratio are not available in the pool, which limits the read on expansion economics. |

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**52 /100 — Mixed/Average.** The explicit weighting is 55% to bank earnings and risk resilience (margin stability 15%, capital intensity 10%, regulatory dependence 15%, rate dependence 5%, cyclicality 10%), 25% to customer economics (pricing power 8%, recurring revenue 9%, stickiness 8%), competitive intensity 10%, industry rate-of-change 5%, and disclosure 5%. That weighting reconstructs to roughly 52 and puts the constraints on a deposit-funded lender ahead of its customer-growth measures.

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Repeat / recurring revenue | 70 | A 139 million-customer base, 83.5% activity rate and US$17 Q2 monthly ARPAC show frequent use of several financial products, although this is not contractual subscription revenue. [Q2’26 earnings presentation, slide 6] |
| Weakest | Regulatory dependence | 35 | Licenses, risk-weighted capital, payment rules and supervisory requirements govern the core business across its products and main markets. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, “Our Regulatory Position”; “Prudential and Capital Requirements”] |

## 4. Read

Nu is a regulated, deposit-funded digital retail bank/lender rather than a subscription-software business; its quality is therefore more credit-, rate- and capital-cycle dependent than its customer-growth figures alone suggest. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5.A, pp.157–158] The single factor to watch over the next 24 months is risk-adjusted NIM — net interest income after credit cost relative to interest-earning assets — alongside NPLs and coverage: its Q2 2026 12.4% level was above the 9.3%–10.8% range in Q1–Q3 2025, so it should not be treated as a through-cycle margin. [Q2’26 earnings presentation, slides 15, 17–19] The Q2 NIM of 22.9% was also above the 18.8%–21.1% range in Q2 2025–Q1 2026; it is a current result, not evidence that credit-cycle risk has disappeared. [Q2’26 earnings presentation, slide 15]
