## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — NU

## 1. Dominant Segment

Nu Group is one reportable segment: digital retail financial services, led by consumer credit, deposits, cards and related fees. It represents 100% of disclosed segment revenue and profit; Brazil produced 91% of the FY2025 geographic-revenue subtotal, so the Brazilian retail-credit market is the relevant competitive arena. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, F-97–F-98]

## 2. Named Competitors

The selected peers are the three listed Brazilian consumer-credit competitors Nu itself names. The LTM revenue and margin figures below are Capital IQ vendor figures in U.S. dollars, presented on that export's financial-institution revenue definitions; they are not interchangeable with Nu's audited IFRS revenue. The return measures are each bank's own 2Q26 managerial or recurring measure.

### Competitor A — Itaú Unibanco Holding S.A.

- **Ticker / listing:** BOVESPA: ITUB4 (also NYSE: ITUB ADR).
- **Where they compete:** Brazilian consumer credit, deposits, credit cards, payments, investments and insurance. Nu names Itaú among its main Brazilian consumer-credit competitors. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D—“Substantial and increasingly intense competition”]
- **Scale:** US$27.594bn LTM total revenue, based on a 5 August 2026 income-statement filing; 3.3 times Nu's US$8.442bn on the same Capital IQ comparable-analysis basis. [Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Financial Data, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export]
- **Profitability / return on capital:** 32.58% LTM net-income margin on the Capital IQ comparable-analysis basis. Its 2Q26 annualized recurring managerial return on average equity (ROE — quarterly earnings relative to shareholders’ average capital) was 24.3%, and recurring managerial profit was R$12.407bn. [Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export; Itaú Unibanco Form 6-K, 2Q26 earnings release, 2026-08-04]
- **Source named in:** Nu’s FY2025 Form 20-F names Itaú as a main Brazilian consumer-credit competitor. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D—“Substantial and increasingly intense competition”]
- **One-line read:** The largest of the three selected listed bank peers, with broad retail products and a R$1.522tn credit portfolio at June 2026. [Itaú Unibanco Form 6-K, 2Q26 earnings release, 2026-08-04]

### Competitor B — Banco Bradesco S.A.

- **Ticker / listing:** BOVESPA: BBDC4 (also NYSE: BBD ADR).
- **Where they compete:** Brazilian consumer credit, cards, deposits, payments, investments and insurance. Nu names Bradesco among its main Brazilian consumer-credit competitors. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D—“Substantial and increasingly intense competition”]
- **Scale:** US$17.910bn LTM total revenue, based on a 5 August 2026 income-statement filing; 2.1 times Nu's US$8.442bn on the same Capital IQ comparable-analysis basis. [Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Financial Data, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export]
- **Profitability / return on capital:** 26.07% LTM net-income margin on the Capital IQ comparable-analysis basis. Its consolidated 2Q26 ROAE was 16.2% and recurring net income was R$7.050bn. [Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export; Banco Bradesco Form 6-K, 2Q26 Economic and Financial Analysis, p.7]
- **Source named in:** Nu’s FY2025 Form 20-F names Bradesco as a main Brazilian consumer-credit competitor. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D—“Substantial and increasingly intense competition”]
- **One-line read:** A full-service incumbent competing for the same retail borrower and depositor while also using insurance and fee income; its 2Q26 expanded loan portfolio was R$1.137tn. [Banco Bradesco Form 6-K, 2Q26 Economic and Financial Analysis, p.7]

### Competitor C — Banco Santander (Brasil) S.A.

- **Ticker / listing:** BOVESPA: SANB11 (also NYSE: BSBR ADR).
- **Where they compete:** Brazilian consumer credit, cards, deposits, payments, investments and insurance. Nu names Santander Brasil among its main Brazilian consumer-credit competitors. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D—“Substantial and increasingly intense competition”]
- **Scale:** US$9.271bn LTM total revenue, based on a 29 July 2026 income-statement filing; 1.1 times Nu's US$8.442bn on the same Capital IQ comparable-analysis basis. [Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Financial Data, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export]
- **Profitability / return on capital:** 28.66% LTM net-income margin on the Capital IQ comparable-analysis basis. Its management-defined recurring ROAE was 12.5% in 2Q26, alongside R$3.0bn recurring managerial net profit. [Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export; Banco Santander (Brasil) Form 6-K, 2Q26 Earnings Release (BR GAAP), p.3]
- **Source named in:** Nu’s FY2025 Form 20-F names Santander Brasil as a main Brazilian consumer-credit competitor. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D—“Substantial and increasingly intense competition”]
- **One-line read:** A scaled incumbent whose 2Q26 consumer-finance, corporate and SME books drove loan growth; its 2Q26 expanded loan portfolio was R$714.769bn. [Banco Santander (Brasil) Form 6-K, 2Q26 Earnings Release (BR GAAP), pp.3, 15]

## 3. Competitive Position

**Position vs peers: Not disclosed.** Nu reports approximately 5% of its Brazil–Mexico–Colombia serviceable market (SAM) for FY2025, but it does not disclose a prior comparable share or a Brazil-only share series. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, p.20] Its FY2025 revenue rose 37% while the company-estimated regional SAM rose 7% (11% FX-neutral), but the measures do not match: Nu's consolidated revenue is not the SAM's stated interest-and-fee revenue net of funding costs. That is not a clean share-gain calculation. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, pp.12, 20] The form names direct competitors but supplies no matched customer, loan-balance or card-volume share series by competitor; a directional share verdict would therefore be inference, not established fact.

## 4. Competitive Shape

Brazilian retail finance has powerful incumbent banks but is not a three-to-five-bank market controlling more than 70% of credit. The Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) classified the 2025 system-wide aggregates as unconcentrated: the four largest institutions held 57.1% of credit operations, and the four leading lenders were Caixa (19.2%), Banco do Brasil (15.4%), Bradesco (11.3%) and Itaú (11.2%). [Banco Central do Brasil, Financial Stability Report, May 2026, pp.66–67] The relevant credit-card market was moderately concentrated rather than an oligopoly: CR4 was 58.1% and the BCB counted 33 effective institutions. [Banco Central do Brasil, Financial Stability Report, May 2026, p.68] Nu's filing calls Brazil concentrated and quotes an HHI of 889 from 2024–25 sources, but that is not the same measure as the BCB's normalized HHI and market-specific CR4 data; the official BCB series is the better basis for the narrower read above. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B—Industry Background; Banco Central do Brasil, Financial Stability Report, May 2026, pp.66–68]

## 5. Caveat

The three selected banks are directly named, public and within roughly 3.3 times Nu's LTM revenue on the same Capital IQ export. This does not exhaust competition: Nu also names Banco Inter, BTG, C6 and XP in investments, and Mercado Pago, PicPay, PagSeguro and StoneCo in payments. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D—“Substantial and increasingly intense competition”] Their product-specific loan, card-spend, active-customer and pricing shares are not disclosed in the material reviewed. A matched Brazil consumer-credit and card-volume share time series for Nu and the named peers would resolve the position-versus-peers gap.

## business-model / 09_moat.md

_Source: `business-model/09_moat.md`_

# Moat — NU

## 1. Named Competitors

- **Itaú Unibanco Holding S.A.** — BOVESPA: ITUB4 / NYSE: ITUB ADR; named by Nu as a Brazilian consumer-credit competitor. Itaú reported a R$1.522tn credit portfolio at June 2026. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D “Substantial and increasingly intense competition”; Itaú Unibanco Form 6-K, 2Q26 earnings release, 2026-08-04]
- **Banco Bradesco S.A.** — BOVESPA: BBDC4 / NYSE: BBD ADR; named by Nu as a Brazilian consumer-credit competitor. Bradesco reported a R$1.137tn expanded loan portfolio in 2Q26. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D “Substantial and increasingly intense competition”; Banco Bradesco Form 6-K, 2Q26 Economic and Financial Analysis, p.7]
- **Banco Santander (Brasil) S.A.** — BOVESPA: SANB11 / NYSE: BSBR ADR; named by Nu as a Brazilian consumer-credit competitor. Santander Brasil reported a R$714.769bn expanded loan portfolio in 2Q26. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D “Substantial and increasingly intense competition”; Banco Santander (Brasil) Form 6-K, 2Q26 Earnings Release, pp.3, 15]

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | Y | Nu had 131.0m customers at FY2025, including 113m in Brazil, and says it was Brazil’s largest private financial institution by customer count. This supports recognition and reach, but the filing does not give a price premium or a retention rate attributable to brand. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, pp.20–21; Item 5.A, p.158] | 55 |
| Cost advantage | Y | NU reported US$7.4 customer-acquisition cost (CAC) in FY2025, 32% paid marketing, and estimates its cost to serve plus G&A per active customer is about 85% below Brazilian incumbents; its 14,314 customers per employee compares with a cited incumbent average of 1,234. The 85% comparison is management’s estimate and is not a like-for-like read on the three named banks. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5.A, p.157] | 65 |
| Distribution | Y | The mobile-led distribution base reached 131.0m customers; Mexico had cash-in/cash-out availability at more than 30,000 physical points. This is broad distribution, though it is not exclusive. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, pp.20–21] | 60 |
| Scale | Y | NU had US$41.9bn deposits acquired directly, 131.0m customers and four products per active customer at FY2025. Yet the named banks remain larger on the comparable-analysis LTM revenue read, so scale is helpful rather than conclusive peer dominance. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5.A, pp.157–159; Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Financial Data, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export] | 60 |
| Technology / IP | Y | The filing describes the proprietary NuCore cloud-based core-banking platform and NuX underwriting engine using proprietary data. No patent portfolio, exclusive technology right, or independently measured credit-loss advantage versus the named peers is disclosed. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B “Technology—Cloud-Based Architecture”; Item 5.A, pp.157–158] | 50 |
| Licenses / regulation | Y | Banking and payment licences are entry barriers, but regulation also promotes Pix, Open Finance and other measures intended to increase competition and innovation. This is a necessary barrier to entry, not a demonstrated NU-specific advantage. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B “Our Regulatory Position” and “Favorable Regulatory Environment”] | 40 |
| Network effects | N | Referral, more customer data and cross-sell may form a feedback loop, but the filing does not establish that each additional customer makes the core account, card or loan product more valuable to other users. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B; Item 5.A, p.158] | 25 |
| Switching costs | Y | Customers held four products per active customer and NU classified more than 62% of active customers as a primary banking relationship at FY2025. The counterweight is material: customers generally have no long-term contracts and deposits may be withdrawn without notice. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, pp.20–21; Item 3.D “Our ability to attract and retain customers…”] | 50 |
| Natural resource access | N | No exclusive natural-resource access is relevant to a digital retail bank/lender. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B “Business Overview”] | 0 |
| Location advantage | N | Brazil generated US$11.038bn, or 91% of FY2025 geographic revenue, which is country concentration rather than an exclusive location advantage. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Note 34, pp.F-97–F-98] | 15 |

## 3. Competitive Economics

NU reports under IFRS in U.S. dollars. For banks, gross and EBIT margins are not a clean common measure: their reported revenue and financial-service costs include funding cost and expected credit loss, while the peer export supplies LTM net-income margins. Those measures are shown only with their labels; they are not interchangeable.

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC, or ROE for financials) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Nu Holdings | 42.0% reported gross margin | Not disclosed as EBIT; closest reported pre-tax margin 24.5% | 17.2% average computed IFRS ROE for FY2022–FY2025; FY2025 alone 30.3% | FY2022–FY2025; FY2025 margin | [FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statement of Profit or Loss, p.155; Item 5.A, p.177; Consolidated Statement of Financial Position, p.157; FY2024 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statement of Changes in Equity] |
| Competitor 1 — Itaú Unibanco | Not disclosed; 32.58% LTM net-income margin on CIQ basis | Not disclosed | 24.3% annualized recurring managerial ROE | 2Q26 / LTM as labelled | [Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export; Itaú Unibanco Form 6-K, 2Q26 earnings release, 2026-08-04] |
| Competitor 2 — Banco Bradesco | Not disclosed; 26.07% LTM net-income margin on CIQ basis | Not disclosed | 16.2% consolidated ROAE | 2Q26 / LTM as labelled | [Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export; Banco Bradesco Form 6-K, 2Q26 Economic and Financial Analysis, p.7] |
| Competitor 3 — Banco Santander (Brasil) | Not disclosed; 28.66% LTM net-income margin on CIQ basis | Not disclosed | 12.5% recurring managerial ROAE | 2Q26 / LTM as labelled | [Capital IQ Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics, as of 2026-08-29 — vendor export; Banco Santander (Brasil) Form 6-K, 2Q26 Earnings Release, p.3] |

The peer ROEs are management-defined current-quarter measures, whereas NU’s 17.2% is a calculated four-year IFRS average. They show directionally that NU is not a clear peer-return outlier; they do not support a precise league table.

**The economic moat test (required).** Return on capital **above** cost of capital: **17.2% average ROE** versus **16.51% cost of equity** (**+68 bps**) — calculated as the simple average of annual IFRS ROEs: FY2022 -7.8%, FY2023 18.2%, FY2024 28.1% and FY2025 30.3%. Each annual ROE is net income attributable to shareholders divided by average total equity; the FY2022 loss is included. The 16.51% is NU’s stated cost of equity for its Brazil-focused Investments activities CGU in the goodwill-impairment test, not a disclosed group-wide cost of equity; it is the only company-disclosed equity hurdle found and therefore limits precision in the comparison. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statements of Profit or Loss and Financial Position, pp.155, 157; FY2024 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statement of Changes in Equity; FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Financial Statements, goodwill impairment analysis, p.F-38]

No group management ROE headline was identified in the audited annual filing; the NU return above is a computed IFRS measure. Tax-rate normalization does not apply because the financial-institution test uses ROE, or net income divided by average equity, rather than NOPAT-based ROIC. The four-year average includes the FY2022 loss, but it is still available-history evidence rather than a fully proven credit-cycle return.

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers — Nu sits at the median of the named peers on the available return measure:** its 17.2% four-year IFRS ROE lies between Itaú’s 24.3% and Santander Brasil’s 12.5% and near Bradesco’s 16.2%. The period and definition differences above mean this is a cautious directional read, and there is insufficient matched gross- or EBIT-margin data to compare named peers.
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test) — the company earns a return on capital above its disclosed cost of equity** (17.2% four-year average ROE versus 16.51%, +68 bps). The narrow gap matters more than the peer ordering.

## 5. Moat Verdict

**Narrow moat — trajectory widening (provisional, not confirmed).** NU’s strongest evidenced advantages are low-cost digital distribution and a large customer/deposit base; they have coincided with returns above the disclosed equity hurdle, but only by 68 bps after including FY2022. The five-year durability test is whether annual IFRS ROE stays above the relevant cost of equity while gross economics and credit losses hold through a weaker Brazilian consumer-credit environment; the business-quality read is mixed on rate of change (50/100), so regulation and digital competition still shorten the period that can be underwritten. [Business Quality — NU, 2026-08-30; FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 3.D]

**Moat trajectory — widening (provisional).**

| Metric (same 3–5 year window) | Start | Latest | Direction | Supports / contradicts the stated trajectory |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Gross margin | 43.5% FY2023 | 42.0% FY2025 | Down 150 bps | Contradicts. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statement of Profit or Loss, p.155; Item 5.A, p.177] |
| EBITDA margin | Not disclosed for this bank | Not disclosed for this bank | Not assessable | Not assessable; EBITDA is not a reported bank performance measure. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statement of Profit or Loss, p.155] |
| EBIT or operating margin | 19.2% FY2023 pre-tax income/revenue; not EBIT | 24.5% FY2025 pre-tax income/revenue; not EBIT | Up 535 bps | Supports, with the bank-specific pre-tax proxy labelled. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statement of Profit or Loss, p.155] |
| Return on capital (ROIC / ROCE) vs cost of capital | FY2022 ROE -7.8% versus 16.51% cost of equity | FY2025 ROE 30.3% versus 16.51% cost of equity | Improved | Supports, but FY2025 alone is not the economic-moat test. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statements of Profit or Loss and Financial Position, pp.155, 157; FY2024 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statement of Changes in Equity; FY2025 Form 20-F, goodwill impairment analysis, p.F-38] |
| Market share (or the closest disclosed volume/position proxy) | Not disclosed | No comparable share series; NU reports about 5% of Brazil–Mexico–Colombia serviceable market in FY2025 | Not assessable | Neither supports nor contradicts. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, p.20] |
| Cash conversion (CFO ÷ EBITDA) | Not meaningful for a bank | Not meaningful for a bank | Not assessable | Lending and deposits drive operating cash flows, and EBITDA is not disclosed; this is not a usable bank cash-conversion test. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows] |
| Pricing / realised price or mix | US$9.8 monthly ARPAC, FY2023 | US$13.3 monthly ARPAC, FY2025 | Up 36% | Supports, but ARPAC can reflect product mix and credit growth as well as price. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Item 5.A, pp.158–159] |

The panel has three supporting financial/customer rows, one contradiction and three metrics that are not assessable. The -150 bps gross-margin move must not be ignored: pre-tax margin rose 535 bps because operating expenses fell from 24.3% of revenue in FY2023 to 17.5% in FY2025, a 680 bps reduction, while gross economics weakened. ARPAC rose 36%, but it does not separate price from product mix or credit growth. Thus the current read is widening on operating leverage and customer monetization, not a confirmed widening of pricing power or market share. [FY2025 Form 20-F, Consolidated Statement of Profit or Loss, p.155; Item 5.A, p.177]

The single data point that would flip this trajectory read is FY2026 IFRS ROE, calculated as net income attributable to shareholders divided by average total equity, falling below the relevant cost of equity. It will be available with the FY2026 annual Form 20-F; the exact filing date is not disclosed in the pool. If it falls below the hurdle, the provisional widening read becomes eroding and the advantage is structure rather than economics.

## business-model / 10_external-dependency.md

_Source: `business-model/10_external-dependency.md`_

# External Dependency Check — NU

## 1. Dependency Table

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interest rates | High | Rates affect consumer spending, credit demand, deposit/funding cost and borrowers’ ability to pay. The earnings effect is not one-way: higher rates can lift interest income but can also reduce payment-fee income and raise funding cost and defaults. Brazilian RDB deposits pay 100% of CDI after 30 days (except fixed-term RDBs), which ties a material funding cost to the local rate. | [FY25 Form 20-F, pp. 132, 166–67, 232]; [H1 FY26 Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 22, p.31] |
| FX | Mid | NU presents in US dollars while its Brazilian, Mexican and Colombian operating entities use BRL, MXN and COP. This creates translation volatility. The June 2026 filing says a portion of the Brazilian net investment is hedged, while FX expenses such as cloud infrastructure are also hedged; it does not establish full protection for the group’s local-currency earnings or equity. | [H1 FY26 Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 2, pp.12–13; Notes 20 and 32, pp.27–30, 42] |
| Government policy | Mid | Brazil’s consumption-tax reform introduces a new financial-services tax regime from 2027, and government monetary, fiscal and exchange-control actions can affect credit availability, funding, consumer purchasing power and cross-border cash flows. The company says the reform’s impact remains under assessment. | [H1 FY26 Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 1.1, p.12]; [FY25 Form 20-F, pp.131–32] |
| Regulation | High | Financial-services operations are regulated in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia. Rules can change capital, liquidity, product and reporting requirements; the interim filing also says local requirements restrict the group’s ability to move assets freely between regulated entities. | [H1 FY26 Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 3, p.14]; [FY25 Form 20-F, Item 3.D, pp.114–15, 165] |
| Consumer cycle | High | The filing states that spending, employment, wages, interest rates and consumer-credit expansion/retraction determine transaction number and value. Brazil supplied US$11.038bn of FY25 revenue out of US$12.084bn total: US$11.038bn / (US$11.038bn + US$0.808bn + US$0.237bn) = 91.4%. That leaves the group highly exposed to Brazilian household credit conditions. | [FY25 Form 20-F, pp.53, 166–67]. CIQ workbook read reconciles after rounding: Brazil US$11,038m (91%), Mexico US$808m (7%) and other countries US$237m (2%) of US$12,084m total. [CIQ Financials→Segments, Geographic Segment → Revenues, 12 months Dec-31-2025 — vendor export] |
| Geopolitics / country risk | Mid | Political, fiscal and social instability in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia can impair local demand, credit performance, funding access and the market price of Brazilian securities. The filing specifically flags Brazil’s October 2026 presidential election as a source of policy uncertainty. | [FY25 Form 20-F, Item 3.D, pp.131–37] |
| Third-party payment and cloud infrastructure | Mid | NU uses Amazon Web Services as its primary third-party cloud provider and incurs Mastercard network/license costs. Service disruption or adverse commercial terms could affect operations; spend, substitutability and supplier concentration are not disclosed, so a High score is not proven. | [FY25 Form 20-F, Item 4.B, Technology—Cloud-Based Architecture; Item 5.A, pp.170–71] |

No direct commodity, freight/logistics, weather or industrial-cycle sensitivity was identified in the filings reviewed. Those variables are not scored Low by default. The CIQ relationship graph covers only recently disclosed customers and suppliers for current subsidiaries. It names AWS and Mastercard but gives no relationship size, contract term or concentration; it therefore cannot support a supplier-concentration conclusion. [CIQ Suppliers/Customers export (NU), retrieved 2026-08-30 — vendor export; `scope_notes` and relationship rows]

## 1A. Named Policy & Subsidy Register — current status as of 2026-08-30

| Programme (local name + English) | Status as of 2026-08-30 | Terms in the reference period | Terms NOW (or successor programme) | Change, quantified | Stated end date? | Source + date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reforma Tributária do Consumo — Consumption Tax Reform: IBS/CBS/IS, Complementary Law 214/2025 as supplemented by Complementary Law 227/2026 | **In force (amended — terms changed)** | PIS/Pasep, Cofins and ISS are the current consumption taxes to be gradually replaced; the interim filing does not disclose a comparable prior effective rate for NU. | Testing begins in 2026. Financial services enter the specific IBS/CBS regime on 2027-01-01 at an estimated 10.85%, rising gradually to 12.50% in 2033; NU says the impact is under assessment. | Stated future rate path: 10.85% initially to 12.50% in 2033 (+165bp). The company does not disclose an old-versus-new effective-tax comparison, so the profit effect is not quantifiable. | No end date stated in the cited sources. | [Brazil Federal Revenue, *Legislação da Reforma Tributária do Consumo*, updated 2026-08-18 — official]; [H1 FY26 Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 1.1, p.12] |
| Resolução BCB nº 246 — Central Bank of Brazil interchange-fee limits | **In force (unchanged)** | The cited disclosure does not provide the prior interchange ceilings or their effect on NU revenue. | A 0.50% maximum applies to domestic debit/deposit-account arrangements; a 0.70% maximum applies to domestic prepaid-payment-account arrangements. The latter provisions took effect 2023-04-01. | 0.50% debit/deposit and 0.70% prepaid ceilings. Change versus the prior regime and NU’s dollar impact are not disclosed. | No end date stated in the official norm. | [Banco Central do Brasil, Resolução BCB nº 246, 2022-09-26, official normative record accessed 2026-08-30]; [FY25 Form 20-F, Item 3.D, p.115] |

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

| Exposure | Disclosed sensitivity | Reported impact | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interest-rate market value | 1bp parallel upward shift in the stated curve; values are US$000 and represent fair-value changes, not an earnings forecast. | As of 2026-06-30: BRL curve (685), COP curve (415), TRY curve (125), MXN curve (59), and US curve +2. | [H1 FY26 Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 32, p.42] |
| FX translation of investments | As of 2025-12-31, a 17.8% USD/BRL shock for Brazilian investments and 10% standard shocks for other currencies. This is an annual-filed sensitivity, not a current unhedged-loss forecast. | FIP Brazil: US$1,369.778m possible change; all listed subsidiaries: US$1,509.598m possible change. The later interim filing designates US$1,370.159m of Brazilian net investment as hedged, but does not publish a replacement FX shock table. | [FY25 Form 20-F, pp.233–34]; [H1 FY26 Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 20, pp.29–30] |

## 3. Classification

**Partly externally driven.** Country macro conditions, consumer credit and regulation are material because 91.4% of FY25 revenue came from Brazil. NU has genuine but partial levers: interest-rate hedges for specified government-bond positions, FX hedges for forecast costs, and a designated hedge for part of the Brazilian net investment. Those measures do not remove dependence on household demand, default conditions, public policy or regulation. [FY25 Form 20-F, pp.53, 166–67]; [H1 FY26 Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Notes 20 and 32, pp.27–30, 42]

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**59/100 — INVERTED: higher = worse.** The score reflects High exposure to rates, consumer credit and regulation, moderated by disclosed hedging and by the absence of a proven direct commodity, freight or weather dependency. It is an external-dependency score, not a forecast of earnings or credit losses.

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

**Brazilian consumer-credit conditions:** a 20% adverse deterioration in borrowers’ capacity to pay would most directly increase expected credit loss and reduce payment activity; the filing does not quantify that 20% scenario. [FY25 Form 20-F, pp.131–32, 166–67, 170–71]

## 2. Classification

**Standard professional management** — the evidence shows a clean audit history, limited disclosed related-party exposure, modest net dilution now offset by buybacks, and no proven serial-acquirer pattern; these positives do not remove the governance constraint from one founder’s voting control or the need to monitor the new CFO and large unused credit limits.

## 3. Most Material Signal

The most material signal is founder control. David Vélez has 74.4% of voting power through super-voting Class B shares, is also CEO and chair, and retains consent rights over material actions including dividends, equity issuance, mergers and acquisitions, and asset transactions above 20% of net equity while the shareholder agreement remains in force [FY2025 Form 20-F, 2025, pp.193 and 203]. This is not evidence of misconduct or of a controller-minority conflict today, but it limits outside holders’ ability to block one if capital allocation or related-party conduct deteriorates; any use of those powers that disadvantages Class A holders would change this classification.

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**65 / 100 — higher = better.** This is the inverse of the weighted severity profile, with the greatest weight on controller power, off-balance-sheet credit commitments, debt funding and dilution. No serial-acquirer cap applies: the available evidence does not show multiple material, debt-funded acquisitions near the company’s own value, and the Banco Porto Real consideration and integration outcome are not disclosed.

## business-model / 12_red-flags-sweep.md

_Source: `business-model/12_red-flags-sweep.md`_

# Red Flags Sweep — NU

## 1. Already Covered Upstream

| Upstream Agent | Flag Already Surfaced |
|---|---|
| disqualifier-scan | No hard disqualifier: clean KPMG opinion, no disclosed restatement or financial-reporting enforcement action; related-party sales/purchases and pledged-share numerator are not assessable. |
| segment-map | One reportable segment and no country-level profit disclosure; Brazil is the economic concentration and credit assets are capital-intensive. |
| customer-geography | Brazil supplied 91.3% of FY2025 geographical revenue; customers have no long-term contracts, but no single customer reached 10% of revenue. |
| business-quality | High regulatory, rate and credit-cycle dependence; payment interchange limits, competitive pressure, and a single operating-segment disclosure constrain the quality read. |
| external-dependency | Brazilian macro, policy, FX, consumer-credit and regulatory exposure, plus third-party cloud and payment-network reliance. |
| capital-allocation-governance | David Vélez's 74.4% voting control, US$38.164bn unused card limits, CFO transition, acquisition execution uncertainty, and the need to reconcile vendor cash-flow data to filings. |

## 2. New Red Flags

| Red Flag | Why It Matters | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = worse)* |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Deferred-tax asset dependence in H1 2026 earnings | The US$991.046m deferred-tax benefit was 51.3% of reported H1 net income of US$1.933bn. It reduced tax expense from US$1.249bn current tax expense to US$258.099m total tax expense: US$1.249bn − US$991.046m = US$258.099m, an 11.8% effective rate on US$2.191bn pre-tax profit. The US$3.649bn net deferred-tax asset is 27.5% of US$13.252bn equity and must be realized against future taxable profit; it is an accounting tax-timing benefit, not cash operating earnings. This is a disclosed IFRS estimate, not evidence of improper accounting. | Gross deferred-tax assets were US$3.806bn: US$3.183bn for credit-loss provisions + US$466.674m other temporary differences + US$156.457m tax-loss carryforwards; less US$156.883m deferred-tax liabilities = US$3.649bn net. The credit-loss component grew through US$1.411bn of H1 constitution, partly offset by US$399.894m realization. [Q2 2026 Unaudited Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Statements of Income, p. 7; Statements of Financial Position, p. 8; Note 30, pp. 36–37] | 62 |
| Rising provision for legal and tax contingencies | The provision balance rose US$13.423m, or 43.4%, in six months to US$44.343m: civil US$30.739m, tax US$8.126m, and labor US$5.478m. H1 additions were US$27.370m versus US$14.474m in H1 2025, while the cash-flow charge for provisions and contingencies was US$25.588m versus US$2.122m. The balance is small beside group earnings, but the increase warrants tracking because civil claims are mainly linked to NuAccount operations and the timing of outflows is uncertain. | Possible but unprovided civil and labor claims were US$4.784m and US$4.891m, respectively. The filing classifies the provisioned claims as probable based on management and internal/external legal counsel. [Q2 2026 Unaudited Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 25, pp. 32–33; Statements of Cash Flows, p. 12] | 42 |

## 3. Most Severe New Flag

The most severe new flag is deferred-tax asset dependence in H1 2026 earnings. The US$991.046m deferred-tax benefit accounts for 51.3% of the reported US$1.933bn H1 net income, while the US$3.649bn net deferred-tax asset equals 27.5% of equity. The filing supports the asset with technical-feasibility studies and each subsidiary's profitability history, so this is not a finding of aggressive accounting. It does mean that the headline tax rate and net income should be read alongside current tax expense and the future realization of credit-loss tax deductions. [Q2 2026 Unaudited Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 30, pp. 36–37; Statements of Income, p. 7; Statements of Financial Position, p. 8]

## 4. Cross-Cutting Patterns

Inference, not from filings: H1 IFRS net income contains two large estimate-driven movements in opposite directions — a US$991.046m deferred-tax benefit raised income while US$25.588m of provisions and contingent liabilities was charged versus US$2.122m a year earlier. This is not an allegation of improper accounting; it makes current-tax expense, deferred-tax-asset realization, and the legal-provision roll-forward more informative than a simple read of headline net income alone. [Q2 2026 Unaudited Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 25, pp. 32–33; Note 30, pp. 36–37; Statements of Cash Flows, p. 12]

## earnings — module synthesis

# Earnings Module — NU (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Nu’s setup is mixed: Q2 revenue and earnings per share (EPS) accelerated, but annual growth slowed and FQ3 favors a miss. [H1 FY26 Interim Statements, p.5]; [FY2025 Form 20-F, F-6–F-7] Card and loan interest supplied 71.6% of Q2 revenue growth as the portfolio grew 37% FX-neutral. [H1 FY26 Interim Statements, Note 6]; [Q2 FY26 deck, slide 13] FQ3 requires 42.3% revenue growth after its estimate rose 7.0% in 90 days, without numeric guidance. [Capital IQ Estimates, FQ3 FY26, current export] The risk is risk expansion, which added 24 basis points (0.24 percentage points) to early delinquency and US$170m to allowances and could reverse the margin gain. [Q2 FY26 transcript, pp.7–8] A vendor-versus-filing cash-flow conflict caps usefulness. Verdict: Mixed earnings setup.

## 1. Earnings Verdict

- **Verdict:** Mixed earnings setup
- Earnings clarity /100 *(higher = better)*: **68** — current primary quarterly data, a verbatim call and consensus support the read, but numeric company guidance and country/product profit are absent. [Earnings Data Triage — NU, §§3–6, 2026-08-30]
- Earnings quality /100 *(higher = better)*: **54** — Material concerns. [Earnings Quality — NU, §9, 2026-08-30]
- Consensus setup /100 *(higher = more beatable)*: **35** — synthesis judgment from the raised FQ3 hurdle, positive revisions and no numeric company guide. [Capital IQ Estimates — Consensus, Trends and Revisions, FQ3/FY2026, current export]
- Earnings volatility /100 *(higher = worse — inverted)*: **68**. [Earnings Sensitivity — NU, §7, 2026-08-30]
- Data quality /100 *(higher = better)*: **80** — the core primary and vendor inputs are present, but detail and one vendor reconciliation are incomplete. [Earnings Data Triage — NU, §§3–6, 2026-08-30]; [Earnings Red Flags — NU, §1, 2026-08-30]
- Overall usefulness /100 *(higher = better)*: **65** — capped because Capital IQ's trailing cash-from-operations figure cannot be reconciled to the filing-built figure. [Earnings Red Flags — NU, §6, 2026-08-30]
- Next-quarter setup: **Favors miss**. [Beat / Miss Setup — NU, §8, 2026-08-30]
- Biggest earnings driver: Credit-card and loan interest increased US$1.320bn year on year and supplied 71.6% of Q2 IFRS revenue growth. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p.14]
- Biggest earnings risk: The same higher-risk credit mix that lifts current interest income can raise expected credit loss (ECL); deliberate risk expansion already added 24 basis points to early delinquency and US$170m to the allowance bridge. [Q2 2026 Earnings Call, prepared remarks, pp.7–8]
- Red-flag severity verdict: **Material concerns**

## 1A. Module Disconfirmation

- **Strongest bear point:** FQ3 consensus requires US$5.937bn of revenue, or 42.3% year-on-year growth, after the estimate rose 7.0% in 90 days; management says originations are normalising and gives no numeric revenue guide. [Capital IQ Estimates — Consensus and Trends, FQ3 2026]; [Q2 2026 Earnings Call, Q&A, pp.9–10]
- **Strongest bull point:** Q2 revenue grew 50.3% and diluted EPS grew 66.3%, while a US$39.4bn portfolio growing 37% FX-neutral can still feed interest income with a lag. [H1 FY2026 Unaudited Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Statement of Income, p.5]; [Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slide 13]
- **Single killer risk:** A credit-cost reversal after the move toward unsecured lending could erase the sequential gain in risk-adjusted net interest margin (NIM after credit costs); the disclosed downside macro state raises ECL by US$504.700m before tax. [Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slides 16 and 18]; [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 3(a), p.15]
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** Q2's acceleration rejects a one-sided deterioration read, but slowing annual revenue growth, negative filing-built trailing cash from operations and rising ECL coverage reject an unqualified acceleration read. [Historical Financials — NU, §§1–2 and 6, 2026-08-30]; [Earnings Quality — NU, §§1–3, 2026-08-30]

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| Specialist | Verdict Line | Biggest Finding |
|---|---|---|
| earnings-data-triage | Sufficient | Audited FY2025, reviewed Q2 2026 statements, a verbatim Q2 call, current consensus and revision history are available; no core partial-data flag applies. [Earnings Data Triage — NU, §§3, 5–6, 2026-08-30] |
| historical-financials | Annual revenue growth is decelerating, while Q2 earnings accelerated | FY2025 revenue growth slowed to 37.0%, but Q2 2026 revenue and diluted EPS rose 50.3% and 66.3%; filing-built trailing cash from operations fell to US$(1.382)bn. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, F-6–F-7 and F-14–F-15]; [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, pp.5 and 12] |
| revenue-drivers | Credit-card and loan interest is the improving main revenue driver | The two lines rose US$1.320bn and explained 35.99 percentage points, or 71.6%, of Q2's 50.29% revenue growth, with no residual in the reported-stream bridge. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, pp.14–15] |
| margin-drivers | Sequential margin improved, but its durability is not proven | Credit income supplied 178 basis points, or 60.5%, of the 294-basis-point sequential rise in risk-adjusted NIM; lower credit cost supplied 115 basis points and the bridge residual was 1 basis point. [Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slide 16] |
| guidance-consensus | Bar is high | FQ3 consensus requires 42.3% revenue growth and 39.0% reported EPS growth; FQ3 revenue estimates rose 7.0% in 90 days. [Capital IQ Estimates — Consensus and Trends, FQ3 2026] |
| beat-miss-setup | Setup favors miss | The raised revenue hurdle and normalising originations outweigh a mixed four-quarter surprise record; earlier credit growth is the main way the call could be wrong. [Beat / Miss Setup — NU, §§7–10, 2026-08-30] |
| earnings-quality | 54/100 — Material concerns | H1 cash from operating activities was US$(1.242)bn, ECL coverage rose 149 basis points to 16.86%, and a US$991.0m deferred-tax benefit lowered the book tax charge. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, pp.5, 12 and 37; Notes 13–14] |
| earnings-sensitivity | 68/100 — higher is worse (inverted) | A 100% downside macro weighting raises ECL by US$504.700m from the weighted allowance; this is a pre-tax allowance bound, not an EPS forecast. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 3(a), p.15] |
| earnings-red-flags | Material concerns | Five High flags converge on one credit-cycle risk: current spread and revenue gains arrive before the full loss outcome is known. [Earnings Red Flags — NU, §§3–6, 2026-08-30] |

## 3. Reconciliation

- **Quarterly acceleration versus annual deceleration:** Historical financials show Q2 revenue and EPS growth of 50.3% and 66.3%, but annual revenue growth slowed from 182.2% in FY2022 to 37.0% in FY2025. The red-flag review therefore rejects a durable acceleration claim. The reconciled view is a strong latest quarter inside a still-unproven longer-term reacceleration, which supports **Mixed earnings setup**. [Historical Financials — NU, §§1, 3 and 6, 2026-08-30]; [Earnings Red Flags — NU, §2.10, 2026-08-30]
- **Sequential margin gain versus adverse counter-series:** Company-defined risk-adjusted NIM rose 294 basis points quarter on quarter, but the implied credit-cost rate was 10.5% versus 8.9% a year earlier. The management efficiency ratio improved to 19.5% from 21.3%, while the different-basis IFRS operating-expense/revenue ratio worsened to 20.1% from 18.2%. These measures are not interchangeable. The reconciled view is a real sequential spread gain with neither credit-cost nor operating-cost durability proven. [Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slides 15–16 and 22]; [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, p.5]
- **Cash-flow source conflict:** The filing-built trailing cash from operating activities (CFO) is US$(1.382)bn, while Capital IQ reports US$(10.305)bn, an unresolved US$8.923bn gap. The reviewed interim and annual filings govern; the vendor figure is not substituted, and the unresolved conflict caps overall usefulness at 65. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Statement of Cash Flows, p.12]; [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, F-14–F-15]; [Capital IQ Financials→Cash Flow, LTM ended 30 June 2026 — vendor export]

## 4. Score Cap Application

| Cap Trigger | Applied? (Y/N) | Affected Score | Final Cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| No quarterly data | N | Earnings clarity | None; max 60 not invoked |
| No consensus / estimate data | N | Consensus setup | None; max 30 not invoked |
| Consensus present but stale | N | Consensus setup | None; no discretionary staleness haircut |
| No cash flow statement | N | Earnings quality | None; max 45 not invoked |
| No revision history | N | Consensus setup | None; max 60 not invoked |
| No verbatim transcript AND no sell-side proxy | N | Earnings clarity | None; max 70 not invoked |
| Transcript role filled ONLY by a sell-side proxy (no verbatim) | N | Earnings clarity | None; max 70 not invoked |
| No segment-level P&L for a multi-segment business | N | Earnings clarity | None; Nu has one disclosed reportable segment |
| Only inferred sensitivities | N | Earnings volatility confidence | No hard cap; allowance sensitivity is company-disclosed, while EPS translation confidence remains Low |
| Conflicting sources not reconcilable | Y | Overall usefulness | **max 65, applied** |

The source-conflict cap is the only applied score cap. No missing-data cap applies. [Earnings Data Triage — NU, §5, 2026-08-30]; [Earnings Red Flags — NU, §6, 2026-08-30]

## 5. Earnings Setup Summary

### Revenue Setup

The next 12 months still have support from a larger credit book and higher revenue per active customer, rather than a disclosed acquisition or divestiture contribution, but Q2's 50.3% reported pace is not proven as a normal run rate. Management says originations are normalising, and Q4 rather than Q3 carries the identified purchase-volume seasonality. [Q2 2026 Earnings Call, Q&A, p.9] The single factor that would flip revenue direction is weaker conversion of credit-card and loan balances into interest income, whether from slower book growth, lower realization or weaker Brazilian consumer credit. Reported IFRS revenue growth of 50.29% differs by 11.29 percentage points from management's 39% FX-neutral gross-revenue growth, but the numerator definitions differ; the gap cannot be called organic growth or FX. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Statement of Income, p.5]; [Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slide 21]

### Margin Setup

Q2's 12.4% company-defined risk-adjusted NIM is an expansion-period result, not a proven cycle peak, floor or normalized margin; management itself said the level was not a floor. [Q2 2026 Earnings Call, Q&A, pp.10–11] Product and country profit are absent, and the filing supplies no earnings coefficient for a 10–20% adverse driver move, so such a stress cannot be quantified without invention. The largest disclosed adverse margin variable is credit cost: a 100% downside macro weighting raises ECL by US$504.700m before tax, while the same risk expansion that helps yield has already raised early delinquency. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 3(a), p.15]; [Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slide 18] Nu has no disclosed automatic cost pass-through or measured realized recovery rate; it can change loan and deposit offers, but that is not proof of broad customer pass-through. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Item 3.D, pp.111–112 and 136]

### Quality Check

The largest current gap between reported and economic earnings is the US$991.0m deferred-tax benefit, equal to 51.3% of H1 net income; it does not prove improper accounting, but it makes the period less cash-backed. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Statement of Income, p.5; Note 30, pp.36–37] Management's adjusted net income also adds back recurring share-based compensation: US$359.0m in FY2025, after US$408.2m in FY2024 and US$289.3m in FY2023. Normalized next-year earnings should therefore start from reported IFRS income and adjust explicit tax timing and credit performance, not start from management's adjusted figure. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Item 5, “Adjusted Net Income (Loss)” reconciliation]

### Consensus Bar

A material beat requires the existing credit book to keep converting into interest income while credit cost and operating spending stay controlled enough to exceed US$6.11484bn of revenue and US$0.23272 of reported EPS, 3% and 5% above consensus. [Beat / Miss Setup — NU, §4, 2026-08-30] The bar looks more likely high than low: revenue consensus rose 7.0% in 90 days, last-month revisions were 8 up / 0 down for FY2026 EPS and 5 up / 2 down for revenue, and management provides no numeric revenue or EPS guide. [Capital IQ Estimates — Trends and Revisions, FQ3/FY2026] The export does not isolate how much of consensus assumes Q2's one-time Desenrola benefit; management said it was a minority of the 115-basis-point sequential credit-cost help, so its exact consensus effect is not proven. [Q2 2026 Earnings Call, Q&A, pp.10–12]

## 5b. Leverage & Capital Structure

Leverage is within normal range and did not change materially during the period — no dedicated treatment required.

## 6. Key Numbers

- Revenue growth rate: Q2 2026 IFRS revenue grew **50.29% year on year** to US$5.513bn; FY2025 annual growth was **37.0%**, down from 43.4% in FY2024. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, p.5]; [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, F-6–F-7]
- EBITDA margin: **Not assessable** — Nu does not report EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization), and interest is core to this lender. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, F-6–F-7]
- EPS: Q2 2026 diluted EPS was **US$0.2162**, up **66.3%** year on year; FQ3 consensus is **US$0.22164**. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, p.5]; [Capital IQ Estimates — Consensus, FQ3 2026]
- CFO / EBITDA: **Not assessable** because EBITDA is absent; H1 cash from operating activities was **US$(1.242)bn** and filing-built trailing CFO was **US$(1.382)bn**. For a lender, these flows include lending, securities and deposit movements. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, p.12]; [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, F-14–F-15]
- Biggest driver current level: Credit-card and loan interest rose **US$1.320bn**, supplying **35.99 percentage points**, or **71.6%**, of Q2 revenue growth. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p.14]
- Consensus gap: No numeric company revenue or EPS guide exists; the FQ3 bar itself requires **42.3% revenue growth** and **39.0% EPS growth** versus Q3 2025. [Capital IQ Estimates — Consensus, FQ3 2026]; [Q2 2026 Earnings Call, Q&A, p.10]
- Estimate revision direction: FY2026 revisions in the last month were **8 up / 0 down for EPS** and **5 up / 2 down for revenue**; FQ3 revenue consensus rose **7.0%** in 90 days. [Capital IQ Estimates — Revisions and Trends, FY2026/FQ3 2026]
- Earnings volatility score: **68/100 — higher is worse (inverted)**; the largest disclosed adverse range is a **US$504.700m** pre-tax ECL increase under 100% downside macro weighting. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 3(a), p.15]

## 7. What Would Change The Earnings Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Upgrade It | What Would Downgrade It | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mixed earnings setup | Move toward **Earnings inflecting — positive** if standalone FQ3 revenue exceeds the material-beat markers of US$6.11484bn and reported EPS of US$0.23272 while early delinquency, ECL coverage and credit cost are stable or better on the same basis as Q2. These markers compare with Q3 2025 revenue of US$4.173bn and EPS of US$0.1595; no reported stub is included. Q1 2026 was within the revenue band but had a material EPS miss (−5.3%), while Q2 was within the revenue band but had a material EPS beat (+15.8%), so the test can fail. [Capital IQ Estimates — Consensus and Surprise, FQ3 2026 and Q1–Q2 2026]; [Beat / Miss Setup — NU, §4, 2026-08-30] | Move toward **Earnings decelerating** if FQ3 revenue falls below the material-miss marker of US$5.75864bn or EPS falls below US$0.21056 while 15–90-day delinquency, ECL coverage or cost of credit worsens, or if transactional and operating costs again grow faster than reported revenue. [Beat / Miss Setup — NU, §4, 2026-08-30]; [Q2 2026 Earnings Presentation, slides 16 and 18] | Standalone FQ3 reported revenue and EPS; same-basis early-delinquency, allowance-coverage, cost-of-credit and efficiency disclosures; and any numeric forward guide. |

## 8. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- Dominant trend: Q2 accelerated, but the annual growth path still slowed; interest income from cards and loans is the main driver.
- Earnings are not cleanly cash-backed: annual cash generation improved through FY2025, but the latest filing-built trailing CFO is negative and lender cash flow is driven by lending, securities and deposits.
- Consensus bar: FQ3 is a raised hurdle with no numeric company revenue or EPS guide; the setup favors miss.
- Next-quarter and look-ahead: FQ3 favors miss; FQ4 may benefit from seasonally higher purchase volume, but no FQ4 bar was carried by the specialist output.
- Top sensitivity: macro-scenario weighting of the credit-loss allowance; current direction is mixed because sequential credit cost improved while ECL and early delinquency remained adverse.
- No missing-data cap applied. The unresolved vendor-versus-filing trailing-CFO conflict limits overall usefulness, and the filing governs.
- Biggest missing data point: country/product profit and credit-cost detail that separates Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, cards and unsecured loans.
- Change the verdict only if FQ3 clears or misses its basis-matched bars together with same-basis evidence on delinquency, ECL coverage, credit cost and efficiency.
- High flag — spread durability: the Q2 gain is exposed to later credit losses from deliberate risk expansion and unsecured mix. [Q2 2026 Earnings Call, pp.7–8]
- High flag — expectations: the FQ3 bar already requires 42.3% revenue growth after upward revisions and has no numeric management support. [Capital IQ Estimates — Consensus and Trends, FQ3 2026]
- High flag — cash and accruals: credit growth consumed cash while ECL coverage rose to 16.86%; this is not proof of fictitious income, but current cash support is not established. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, p.12; Notes 13–14]
- High flag — tax quality: the US$991.046m deferred-tax benefit represented 51.3% of H1 net income; this is not evidence of improper accounting. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, p.5; Note 30, pp.36–37]
- High flag — macro sensitivity: 100% downside macro weighting raises the allowance by US$504.700m from the weighted case; this is a pre-tax allowance bound, not an EPS forecast. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 3(a), p.15]
- Red-flag severity verdict: **Material concerns**
- RF-EQ-001 (rising accruals divergent from cash earnings)

## 9. Simple Summary

- Revenue accelerated in Q2, but annual growth has been slowing.
- Card and loan interest drove most of the latest revenue increase.
- Risk-adjusted margin improved, but higher-risk lending can raise later losses.
- Reported IFRS income is a better starting point than adjusted income because share-based compensation recurs.
- The FQ3 consensus bar is hard to beat, and the setup favors miss.
- Credit-loss assumptions are the largest disclosed earnings sensitivity.
- Earnings volatility is high, and the cash and tax signals need caution.
- The module is useful to the master synthesizer, but the unresolved vendor cash-flow conflict caps that usefulness.

# Historical Financials — NU

Nu Holdings Ltd. reports under IFRS Accounting Standards in U.S. dollars and has a 31 December fiscal year. Amounts below are US$ millions unless stated otherwise. `Total revenue` is the audited IFRS line before funding cost, transactional expense and expected credit loss; it is not Capital IQ's bank-template `Total Revenue` label.

Parentheses in the net-debt row denote net cash. Strict cash basis means filing cash and cash equivalents less the debt scope stated below; it does not net securities or other liquid investments. The debt build is borrowings and financing, excluding operating lease liabilities, which the filings present separately. FY2021 additionally includes US$10.0m of separately disclosed securitized borrowings. Repurchase agreements are also separately presented and are not included in this supporting historical-financials measure; the balance-sheet-survival module should perform the canonical debt-scope assessment. A net-debt/EBITDA ratio is not meaningful here because Nu does not report EBITDA and interest income and funding cost are core banking operations. [1][2][3]

FCF is defined as CFO less cash payments for property, plant and equipment and intangible assets. For a lender, it is heavily affected by lending, securities, deposits and other balance-sheet movements; it is not presented as distributable cash. [1][2]

Net debt is a point-in-time measure. At 30 June 2026, the build is US$4,682.3m borrowings and financing less US$13,551.6m cash and cash equivalents = US$(8,869.4)m. The debt note confirms that the US$4,682.3m excludes the separately shown US$66.4m operating lease liability; it comprises US$2,814.3m financial bills and US$1,867.9m margin-loan facility. [4]

**Capital IQ sidecar reconciliation.** The sidecar's present FY2025 `Revenue` value is US$6,991.185m, whereas audited IFRS total revenue is US$15,774.741m. This is not the same measure: US$15,774.741m − US$4,578.680m interest and other financial expenses − US$4,204.876m expected credit loss = US$6,991.185m; it is before US$366.183m transactional expenses and therefore neither audited total revenue nor gross profit. [1][9] The sidecar also reports LTM cash from operations of US$(10,304.8)m versus the filing-built US$(1,381.6)m above; this US$8,923.2m difference is material and is flagged as an incompatible vendor cash-flow presentation, not silently substituted. [4][9] Its US$(9,274.2)m net-debt figure at 30 June 2026 is a vendor basis that may net liquid investments; it differs from this report's filing-built strict US$(8,869.4)m by US$404.8m. The CIQ total-debt value is US$5,896.7m versus the filing debt-note scope of US$4,682.3m, so the vendor figure cannot be used as a filing-clean strict-net-debt measure. [4][9]

## 5. Quarterly Seasonality Table (last 3 fiscal years)

*Insufficient quarterly history for seasonality analysis.* The pool does not contain three full fiscal years of like-for-like, primary quarterly financial statements; no quarterly revenue-share or margin seasonality conclusion is made.

## 6. Key Trend Summary

Revenue growth remains positive but is decelerating on the annual base: 182.2% in FY2022, 67.5% in FY2023, 43.4% in FY2024 and 37.0% in FY2025. [1][2][8] Gross margin is volatile: it recovered from 34.7% in FY2022 to 45.6% in FY2024, then fell 361bp to 42.0% in FY2025; the latest quarter improved 37bp year on year to 42.6%, after Q1 2026's 37.5%. [1][4][8] Reported net income and diluted EPS changed from losses in FY2021–22 to US$2.869bn and US$0.5846 in FY2025, but operating cash flow is the counter-series: it was US$(1.242)bn in H1 2026 and the filing-built TTM was US$(1.382)bn despite rising income. [1][2][4][8] Material quarterly seasonality is not proven from the available record.

# Revenue Drivers — NU

Nu Holdings reports under IFRS Accounting Standards in U.S. dollars and has a 31 December year-end. Unless stated otherwise, figures below are US$ and relate to the reported IFRS revenue line. Management's portfolio, ARPAC, NIM and gross-revenue measures are separately labelled as management measures or non-IFRS.

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

Single-segment business (>85% from one segment) — consolidated analysis. Nu reports one reportable segment, the Nu Group, which was 100% of FY2025 audited IFRS revenue of US$15.775bn. Product and country profit are not disclosed, so this report does not invent them. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Note 34, F-97–F-98; business-model segment map, 2026-08-30]

Capital IQ's present sidecar read is `Banking US$6.991bn (100%) of Total US$6.991bn` [CIQ Financials→Segments (Revenues, latest annual column), 12 months ended 31 December 2025 — vendor export]. This is not a second segment or audited IFRS revenue: it reconciles to US$15.775bn IFRS revenue less US$4.579bn interest and other financial expenses less US$4.205bn expected credit loss = US$6.991bn. The vendor's bank-template measure is therefore not used as revenue in this report. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Statement of Income, F-7; Note 34, F-97]

## 2. Revenue Driver Tree

| Business Type | Revenue Formula |
|---|---|
| Lender / digital bank | Loan and card receivables × effective yield, plus interest on other earning assets and financial-instrument gains/losses, plus card purchase volume × interchange and other fees |

Company-specific formula: **IFRS total revenue = interest and gains on credit-card receivables, loans and other financial assets + card/prepaid interchange income, late fees, insurance commissions and other fees.** Credit-card interchange is linked to transaction value and merchant-segment rates; interest on revolving/instalment card balances and loans uses the effective-interest method. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Item 5, pp. 157–158; Note 6, F-39]

The bank/lender overlay is applied. NIM, loan growth, deposit growth, NPLs, credit cost, coverage, CAR and ROE are available; standard CASA/funding mix and group ROA are not disclosed. Deposits and their cost are not a substitute for CASA. [business-model/02_business-identity.md, §3a, 2026-08-30]

## 3. Market / Share / Price / Mix Split

|---|---|---|---:|
| End-market demand | Mixed; lending and activity are expanding, but Brazil household credit conditions and rates remain material | Q2 2026 total credit portfolio reached US$39.4bn, +37% YoY FX-neutral; management states that spending, employment, rates and credit availability affect activity and demand. Brazil supplied US$11.038bn, or 91.4%, of FY2025's narrower US$12.084bn geographic-revenue disclosure; this is not the US$15.775bn consolidated IFRS revenue line. The filing says card income is linked to credit/prepaid purchase volume and merchant-segment interchange rates. Deposit growth supports balance-sheet capacity, but the standard CASA split is absent. [Q2'26 Earnings Presentation, slide 14; H1 FY2026 Unaudited Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 14; business-model/02_business-identity.md, §3a, 2026-08-30] |
| Mexico and Colombia product expansion | Mexico had 16.0m customers at July 2026; country revenue/profit for Q2 is not disclosed | Improving | Low today / Mid over time | Mexico's full-bank authorisation enables payroll deposits, broader credit, higher deposit insurance and new segments. Its current consolidated revenue contribution cannot be quantified: FY2025 geographic revenue was only disclosed on a narrower basis, with Mexico US$808m (7%) and other countries US$237m (2%). [Q2'26 Earnings Presentation, slide 8; Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Note 34(b), F-98; CIQ Financials→Segments, Geographic Segment → Revenues, 12 months ended 31 December 2025 — vendor export] |

**Cycle position:** *mid-cycle lending expansion — inference, not from filings.* The latest portfolio is still growing 37% YoY FX-neutral, but management says QoQ origination is normalising after an unusually fast expansion and that Q1 balances matured into Q2 income. Nu also reports seasonally higher Q4 purchase volume and revenue. With no reported earlier credit-cycle peak/trough series in the pool, peak versus trough is not assessable; Q2's revenue pace is not a normalised run rate. This is consistent with the business-model module's finding that consumer credit and rates are high external dependencies. [Q2 2026 Earnings Call transcript, prepared remarks and Q&A, pp. 6, 9; H1 FY2026 Unaudited Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 1, p. 12; business-model/10_external-dependency.md, §§1, 3, 2026-08-30]

## 5. Revenue Drivers By Segment (if applicable)

Not applicable beyond the Nu Group: it is the sole reportable segment. Brazil, Mexico and Colombia are operating geographies, not disclosed profit segments. The FY2025 geographic-revenue table has a narrower scope than consolidated IFRS revenue, so it cannot be used to allocate Q2 consolidated revenue or profit. [Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Note 34, F-97–F-98]

## 6. Revenue Growth Decomposition

Q2 2026 IFRS total revenue was US$5,513.208m versus US$3,668.470m in Q2 2025: a US$1,844.738m increase, or **50.29%**. This bridge uses reported income-statement categories, not management's US$5.876bn Q2 gross-revenue measure. [H1 FY2026 Unaudited Interim Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements, Statement of Income, p. 5; Note 6, pp. 14–15; Q2'26 Earnings Presentation, slide 21]

| Component | Contribution to Growth (pp) | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Credit-card interest income | 19.46 | US$1,805.581m less US$1,091.598m = US$713.983m; reported Note 6 line. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 14] |
| Loan interest income | 16.53 | US$1,734.365m less US$1,128.020m = US$606.345m; reported Note 6 line. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 14] |
| Other interest income and financial-instrument gains | 8.49 | Other assets at amortized cost +US$266.729m; other receivables -US$5.828m; fair-value financial instruments +US$67.339m; other fair-value income -US$16.738m. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 14] |
| Credit and prepaid-card fee income | 3.88 | US$534.970m less US$392.568m = US$142.402m. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 15] |
| Late fees | 1.27 | US$136.801m less US$90.193m = US$46.608m. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 15] |
| Insurance and other fee income | 0.65 | Insurance +US$1.916m and other fees +US$21.982m. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 15] |
| Total revenue growth | **50.29** | US$1,844.738m ÷ US$3,668.470m Q2 2025 IFRS revenue. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Statement of Income, p. 5] |

The filing does not disclose a same-basis volume × yield × mix bridge for its IFRS revenue categories. The table therefore identifies the reported income streams that moved revenue; it does not claim that the card/loan-interest contribution is purely volume, price, or mix.

## 6a. Decomposition Attribution and Residual (MODULE_RULES "Driver Attribution" / §15)

All pp contributions use the same reported Q2 2025 IFRS revenue denominator, US$3,668.470m. They are **asserted from disclosure, no quoted volume/price/mix ratio applied**:

```text
Credit-card interest: (US$1,805.581m − US$1,091.598m) ÷ US$3,668.470m [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 14]
  = 19.46pp of the 50.29pp observed growth
  → no volume/price/mix ratio applied

Loan interest: (US$1,734.365m − US$1,128.020m) ÷ US$3,668.470m [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 14]
  = 16.53pp of the 50.29pp observed growth
  → no volume/price/mix ratio applied

Other interest and gains: US$311.502m net reported change ÷ US$3,668.470m [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 14]
  = 8.49pp of the 50.29pp observed growth
  → no volume/price/mix ratio applied

Credit/prepaid-card fees: (US$534.970m − US$392.568m) ÷ US$3,668.470m [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 15]
  = 3.88pp of the 50.29pp observed growth
  → no volume/price/mix ratio applied

Late fees: (US$136.801m − US$90.193m) ÷ US$3,668.470m [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 15]
  = 1.27pp of the 50.29pp observed growth
  → no volume/price/mix ratio applied

Insurance and other fees: US$23.898m net reported change ÷ US$3,668.470m [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 15]
  = 0.65pp of the 50.29pp observed growth
  → no volume/price/mix ratio applied
```

Reconciliation: 19.46 + 16.53 + 8.49 + 3.88 + 1.27 + 0.65 = **50.29pp reconciled, 0.00pp residual** (rounding to two decimals). The resulting attribution is a reported revenue-stream bridge, not a causal price/volume decomposition.

## 7. The Single Biggest Revenue Driver

**Interest income from the credit-card and loan book is the single biggest revenue driver, and it is improving.** Its US$1.320bn year-on-year increase equals 35.99pp, or 71.6%, of Q2's 50.29% IFRS revenue growth, so it clears the "main driver" test on the reported bridge. The underlying management portfolio grew 37% YoY FX-neutral to US$39.4bn, led by cards and unsecured lending; management says Q1 balance growth matured into Q2 income. That leaves the revenue driver exposed to Brazilian consumer-credit conditions, rates, underwriting and mix: Brazil represented 91.4% of the filing's narrower FY2025 geographic-revenue table, and the standard CASA mix is still not disclosed. Q4's holiday purchase-volume seasonality and the recognised lag from originations mean the current Q2 pace should not be treated as a normalised run rate. [H1 FY2026 Interim Financial Statements, Note 6, p. 14; Q2'26 Earnings Presentation, slide 13; Q2 2026 Earnings Call transcript, prepared remarks and Q&A, pp. 6, 9; Nu Holdings Ltd., Form 20-F, FY2025, Note 34(b), F-98]
